• Cis-acting: DNA sequences located on the same molecule as the gene (e.g., TATA box, HREs)
• Trans-acting: Diffusible molecules (usually proteins) that bind to DNA (e.g., transcription factors, receptors)

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the base modification and linkage type required to stabilize the 5' end of eukaryotic pre-mRNA.
back:
• 7-methylguanosine cap
• 5'-to-5' triphosphate linkage
• Protects mRNA from 5' exonucleases
• Essential for recognition by the ribosome during translation initiation

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: The fundamental structural unit of eukaryotic chromatin, consisting of DNA wrapped around an octamer of histone proteins, is called the [___].
back:
Nucleosome.
• Formed by DNA coiling twice around two molecules each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
• Joined by linker DNA and stabilized by H1 histone.
• Facilitates the compacting of genomic DNA into chromosomes.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In an E. coli culture, glucose is depleted but lactose is abundant. Identify the status of the lac repressor and the specific role of allolactose in this scenario.
back:
Allolactose acts as an inducer.
• It binds to the lac repressor, changing its conformation so it cannot bind the operator.
• This removes the physical block on RNA polymerase.
• Results in maximal transcription of structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA).

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain how histone acetylation by Histone Acetyltransferases (HATs) facilitates the activation of gene expression.
back:
Acetylation removes the positive charge from lysine residues.
• Weakens ionic interactions between histones and negatively charged DNA.
• Chromatin decondenses into euchromatin.
• Enhances accessibility for transcription factors and RNA polymerase to bind DNA.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the molecular mechanisms that produce full-length Apolipoprotein B-100 in the liver with the shorter B-48 isoform in the intestine.
back:
Post-transcriptional RNA editing.
• Liver: No editing; full-length mRNA translated to Apo B-100.
• Intestine: Cytosine-to-uracil deamination changes a glutamine codon to a stop codon (UAA).
• Result: Truncated protein representing 48% of the gene sequence.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the unique properties of eukaryotic enhancers that distinguish them from core promoter sequences.
back:
Distal regulatory elements.
• Position-independent (upstream or downstream of the gene).
• Distance-independent (can be thousands of base pairs away).
• Function in either orientation by looping DNA to interact with the promoter.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In eukaryotic protein-coding genes, the core promoter consensus sequence (TATAAA) that recruits General Transcription Factors is the [___].
back:
TATA or Hogness box.
• Located ~25 base pairs upstream of the start site.
• Recognized by TFIID (via TATA-binding protein).
• Critical for the assembly of the preinitiation complex and RNA polymerase II.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A patient with iron deficiency anemia shows increased transferrin receptor (TfR) synthesis. Explain the interaction between IRPs and IREs in this metabolic state.
back:
3'-UTR mRNA stabilization.
• Low iron allows Iron Regulatory Proteins (IRPs) to bind Iron Responsive Elements (IREs) on TfR mRNA.
• Binding prevents mRNA degradation by nucleases.
• Increased mRNA stability leads to higher TfR translation to capture plasma iron.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the mechanism of transcriptional attenuation in the bacterial trp operon when tryptophan levels are high.
back:
Premature termination of transcription.
• Ribosome moves rapidly through the leader sequence, allowing a 3-4 stem-loop to form.
• This attenuator structure acts as a rho-independent termination signal.
• Prevents synthesis of the full polycistronic mRNA for tryptophan biosynthesis.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Differentiate between euchromatin and heterochromatin regarding their physical state and transcriptional activity.
back:
Euchromatin: Decondensed, acetylated, and transcriptionally active.
• Heterochromatin: Highly condensed, methylated (often), and transcriptionally silent.
• Heterochromatin is found at centromeres and is often associated with gene silencing.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the primary role of the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) in the regulation of eukaryotic gene expression.
back:
Post-transcriptional gene silencing.
• Uses a microRNA (miRNA) guide strand to find complementary target mRNA.
• Induces mRNA cleavage or inhibits translation.
• Regulates processes like cell differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In eukaryotic gene transcription, the [___] box is the specific cis-acting core promoter sequence located approximately 25 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site.
back:
*   TATA box (Hogness box)
*   Recognized by TFIID (TATA-binding protein)
*   Determines the precise start site
*   Essential for recruiting RNA polymerase II

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A patient presents with a chronic neurodegenerative disorder caused by tandem repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene. Identify the specific type of mutation that results in an abnormally long polyglutamine tract.
back:
*   Trinucleotide repeat expansion
*   Specifically CAG repeats
*   Causes protein aggregation and neurotoxicity
*   Leads to toxic gain-of-function in Huntington disease

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the conformational response of the prokaryotic lac repressor when it encounters the inducer allolactose.
back:
*   Allolactose binds to the repressor protein
*   Induces a conformational change
*   Reduces affinity for the operator site
*   Allows RNA polymerase to initiate transcription

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the DNA organization and coding capacity of a prokaryotic operon with a typical eukaryotic protein-coding gene.
back:
*   Prokaryotic operon: Polycistronic (multiple genes, single transcript)
*   Eukaryotic gene: Monocistronic (one gene, single transcript)
*   Eukaryotes contain introns; Prokaryotes generally do not

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: State the biochemical effect of histone acetyltransferases (HATs) on chromatin accessibility.
back:
*   Adds acetyl groups to lysine residues
*   Neutralizes positive charge on histones
*   Weakens histone-DNA interaction
*   Decondenses chromatin into transcriptionally active Euchromatin

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In the regulation of the tryptophan operon, the stalling of ribosomes at Trp codons during low amino acid levels prevents the formation of the [___] hairpin.
back:
*   Attenuator (Termination hairpin)
*   Allows transcription to continue to completion
*   Mediates transcriptional attenuation
*   Specific to coupled transcription-translation systems

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A 40-year-old male with a family history of Lynch syndrome is diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Identify the post-replication gene regulation/repair mechanism that is defective in this individual.
back:
*   Mismatch Repair (MMR)
*   Mutations in MSH2 or MLH1
*   Corrects errors that escaped polymerase proofreading
*   Reduces mutation rates significantly

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain the mechanism of post-transcriptional regulation of transferrin receptor synthesis when intracellular iron levels are low.
back:
*   Iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) bind 3'-IREs
*   Binding stabilizes the mRNA molecule
*   Prevents mRNA degradation by nucleases
*   Leads to increased transferrin receptor translation

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distinguish between cis-acting elements and trans-acting factors in eukaryotic gene regulation.
back:
*   Cis-acting: DNA sequences on same chromosome (e.g., Enhancers)
*   Trans-acting: Diffusible molecules (e.g., Transcription Factors)
*   Trans-acting factors transit from cytoplasm to DNA

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Name the specific noncoding RNA species that mediates gene silencing by either repressing translation or increasing mRNA degradation in the cytoplasm.
back:
*   MicroRNA (miRNA)
*   Derived from primary miRNA (pri-miRNA)
*   Associates with the RISC complex
*   Pairs with 3'-UTR of target mRNA

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In eukaryotic gene transcription, the core promoter consensus sequence [___] is located approximately 25 nucleotides upstream of the start site and serves as a primary binding site for TFIID.
back:
*   **TATA box** (Hogness box)
*   High in Adenine and Thymine content
*   Directs RNA polymerase II to the correct start site and facilitates DNA strand melting

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A child is diagnosed with β-thalassemia. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation at the GU invariant sequence within the first intron of the β-globin gene. Identify the molecular process primarily impaired by this mutation.
back:
*   **RNA Splicing**
*   The mutation disrupts the splice donor site recognized by snRNPs (U1)
*   Results in aberrant mRNA through exon skipping or intron retention, preventing functional globin synthesis

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain the mechanism by which allolactose facilitates the induction of the lac operon structural genes in E. coli.
back:
*   Acts as an **inducer** by binding to the **lac repressor** protein
*   Causes a conformational change that prevents the repressor from binding the operator
*   Relieves negative inhibition, allowing RNA polymerase to transcribe the operon

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the nature and functional scope of cis-acting DNA elements with trans-acting regulatory factors in human gene expression.
back:
*   **Cis-acting:** Intrinsic DNA sequences (promoters, enhancers) that regulate genes on the same physical chromosome.
*   **Trans-acting:** Diffusible molecules (transcription factors) synthesized elsewhere that travel to bind specific DNA target motifs.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Summarize the unique properties of enhancers regarding their spatial orientation and distance from the target gene promoter.
back:
*   **Distance-independent:** Can be thousands of base pairs away
*   **Position-flexible:** Located 5', 3', or within introns
*   **Orientation-independent:** Function effectively in either forward or reverse direction

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: The fundamental structural unit of eukaryotic chromatin, comprising a DNA segment wound twice around an octamer of basic histone proteins, is the [___].
back:
*   **Nucleosome**
*   Histone octamer: Pairs of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
*   **H1 histone** serves as the linker protein between consecutive beads

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A patient’s liver produces apolipoprotein B-100, while their intestine produces a shorter B-48 isoform from the same gene. Describe the post-transcriptional mechanism responsible for this tissue-specific variation.
back:
*   **RNA Editing**
*   Cytidine deaminase converts Cytosine to Uracil (CAA to UAA stop codon) specifically in the intestine
*   Results in a truncated protein with distinct physiological functions in lipid transport

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Detail the molecular mechanism by which intracellular iron deficiency leads to increased synthesis of the transferrin receptor (TfR).
back:
*   **Iron Regulatory Proteins (IRP)** bind to **Iron-Responsive Elements (IRE)** at the 3'-UTR of TfR mRNA
*   Binding stabilizes the mRNA, preventing its degradation
*   Leads to increased translation and higher iron uptake capacity

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distinguish between euchromatin and heterochromatin regarding their histone acetylation status and transcriptional availability.
back:
*   **Euchromatin:** Highly acetylated (reduced positive charge), decondensed, and transcriptionally active.
*   **Heterochromatin:** Deacetylated and/or methylated, highly condensed, and transcriptionally silent (inaccessible to RNA polymerase).

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the structural arrangement in prokaryotes where functionally related genes are grouped and transcribed as a single polycistronic mRNA.
back:
*   **Operon**
*   Components: Promoter, Operator, and Structural genes
*   Ensures **coordinate regulation**, allowing the cell to turn metabolic pathways on/off as a single unit

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In the organization of a eukaryotic gene, the non-coding segments that are transcribed into the primary RNA but removed during processing are called [___].
back:
* Introns.
* These sequences are excised by the spliceosome during mRNA maturation.
* The remaining segments, exons, are ligated together to form the final protein-coding sequence.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In an experimental setup, Escherichia coli cells are grown in a medium containing lactose but no glucose. Describe the resulting transcriptional state of the lac operon structural genes.
back:
* Maximally expressed (induced).
* Allolactose binds the repressor, preventing it from blocking the operator.
* Absence of glucose ensures high cAMP levels, activating the CAP protein to facilitate RNA polymerase binding.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain how the 'beads-on-a-string' organization of eukaryotic DNA is formed.
back:
* DNA winds approximately 1.7 times around an octameric core of histones.
* The octamer consists of pairs of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 proteins.
* This bead-like structure, the nucleosome, is the fundamental unit of chromatin.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the molecular consequences of a mutation occurring in a gene's promoter region with one occurring at a splice donor site.
back:
* Promoter mutations decrease the total amount of mRNA synthesized, causing quantitative deficiency.
* Splice site mutations produce aberrant mRNA through exon skipping or intron retention.
* Promoter issues affect initiation; splice issues affect post-transcriptional processing.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the mechanism by which the antibiotic Rifampin inhibits bacterial gene expression.
back:
* Binds to the beta subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase.
* Prevents the initiation of transcription by blocking the formation of the first phosphodiester bonds.
* Does not affect eukaryotic RNA polymerase, ensuring selective toxicity.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: The term used to describe a single prokaryotic mRNA molecule that contains the coding information for multiple functionally related proteins is [___].
back:
* Polycistronic.
* This arrangement allows for the coordinate regulation of an entire operon.
* Translation occurs at multiple internal sites, producing distinct protein products from a single transcript.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A patient's biopsy reveals that tumor suppressor genes are silenced despite having a normal DNA sequence. The laboratory identifies dense methylation of cytosine residues in the promoter region. Name this regulatory mechanism.
back:
* Epigenetic silencing.
* Involves chemical modifications like DNA methylation or histone deacetylation that inhibit expression.
* These changes are heritable through cell division but do not alter the underlying nucleotide sequence.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the mechanism of 'Attenuation' in the regulation of the prokaryotic Tryptophan (trp) operon.
back:
* Ribosomes stall at specific codons when the amino acid is scarce.
* This prevents the formation of an mRNA hairpin that terminates transcription.
* Consequently, transcription continues through the structural genes only when amino acid levels are low.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distinguish between cis-acting elements and trans-acting factors in the regulation of eukaryotic transcription.
back:
* Cis-acting elements are non-coding DNA sequences (e.g., enhancers) on the same chromosome.
* Trans-acting factors are diffusible proteins (e.g., transcription factors) that bind to these sequences.
* Cis-acting sites are fixed; trans-acting factors travel to their targets.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the specific histone protein that is NOT part of the nucleosome core but instead binds to the linker DNA.
back:
* Histone H1.
* It binds to the linker DNA region between individual nucleosome beads.
* Its primary role is to stabilize the higher-order folding of chromatin into 30-nm fibers.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In eukaryotic gene structure, the non-coding intervening sequences that are initially transcribed but later removed during processing are called [___].
back:
• Introns.
• Removed via the spliceosome complex.
• Join exons together to form mature, coding mRNA.
• Rare or absent in most prokaryotic genes.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A lab culture of E. coli is grown in a medium containing both glucose and lactose. Despite lactose presence, the lac operon remains uninduced. Explain the biochemical mechanism.
back:
• Catabolite Repression.
• High glucose inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP levels.
• Absence of cAMP-CAP complex prevents RNA polymerase binding.
• Ensures glucose is utilized preferentially over lactose.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Detail the biochemical mechanism by which histone acetylation facilitates eukaryotic gene transcription.
back:
• Catalyzed by Histone Acetyltransferases (HATs).
• Attaches acetyl groups to N-terminal lysine residues.
• Neutralizes positive charges, weakening histone-DNA affinity.
• Relaxes chromatin into euchromatin, allowing transcription factor access.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the spatial and directional requirements of eukaryotic promoters with those of enhancer elements.
back:
• Promoters: Position-dependent; located immediately upstream (5') of start site (+1).
• Enhancers: Position-independent; can be upstream, downstream, or distal.
• Orientation: Enhancers function in either forward or reverse orientation.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the process of attenuation in the Trp operon when intracellular tryptophan levels are high.
back:
• Premature transcription termination.
• Ribosomes rapidly translate the leader peptide.
• Favors formation of 3-4 hairpin (attenuator) stem-loop.
• Causes RNA polymerase dissociation before transcribing structural genes.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: The core eukaryotic promoter element located approximately 25 nucleotides upstream of the transcription start site is the [___].
back:
• TATA Box (Hogness Box).
• Consensus sequence is TATAAA.
• Serves as the binding site for TFIID (General Transcription Factor).
• Facilitates the melting of the DNA double helix.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Molecular analysis of intestinal Apolipoprotein B reveals it is only 48% the length of the hepatic version. Identify the specific post-transcriptional mechanism.
back:
• RNA Editing.
• Enzyme deaminates Cytosine to Uracil (C-to-U) in mRNA.
• Converts Gln codon (CAA) to Stop codon (UAA).
• Results in tissue-specific protein truncation (Apo B-48).

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain how microRNAs (miRNA) carry out the biological function of gene silencing within the cytoplasm.
back:
• miRNA associates with RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC).
• Guide strand hybridizes to target mRNA 3'-UTR.
• Results in mRNA degradation (high complementarity).
• Or results in translation repression (partial complementarity).

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distinguish between cis-acting elements and trans-acting factors in the context of gene regulation.
back:
• Cis-acting: Specific DNA sequences (e.g., operators, promoters) on the same chromosome.
• Trans-acting: Diffusible molecules (e.g., STFs, repressors) synthesized elsewhere.
• Interaction: Trans-factors bind cis-elements to regulate expression.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the signal sequence and the enzyme responsible for the template-independent addition of the 3' poly-A tail in eukaryotes.
back:
• Signal: AAUAAA consensus sequence near 3' end.
• Enzyme: Polyadenylate Polymerase.
• Uses ATP as substrate.
• Functions to stabilize mRNA and facilitate nuclear export.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In eukaryotic gene structure, the non-coding intervening sequences that are removed during RNA splicing are called [___].
back: - Introns; - Removed by spliceosomes; - Do not appear in mature mRNA; - Flanked by expressed sequences (exons).

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A 45-year-old male is diagnosed with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome). The underlying genetic defect involves a failure in the [___] repair system.
back: - Mismatch Repair (MMR); - Corrects errors escaping proofreading; - Discriminates strands via hemimethylation in prokaryotes; - Involves MSH2 or MLH1 mutations.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain the mechanism by which the Lac repressor protein inhibits transcription in E. coli when glucose is the sole carbon source.
back: - Repressor binds to the operator (O) site; - Physically blocks RNA polymerase binding; - Prevents transcription of structural genes (Z, Y, A); - Example of negative regulation.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the spatial and functional characteristics of eukaryotic enhancers with core promoter elements.
back: - Promoters: Fixed position (upstream), bind general factors (GTFs); - Enhancers: Variable position (distal), bind specific activators; - Enhancers increase initiation rate via DNA looping.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the process of attenuation in the regulation of the prokaryotic tryptophan (trp) operon.
back: - Transcription stops prematurely before structural genes; - Dependent on rapid translation or ribosome stalling; - Mediated by mRNA hairpin (stem-loop) structures; - Couples transcription and translation.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: The transcriptionally active, decondensed form of chromatin that allows access to the transcriptional machinery is known as [___].
back: - Euchromatin; - Highly acetylated histones; - Less methylated DNA (hypomethylated); - Relaxed nucleosome structure.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A child presents with severe anemia. Genetic testing reveals a mutation at an invariant GU sequence at the start of an intron. Identify the likely molecular consequence.
back: - Splice site mutation; - Results in improper intron removal; - May cause exon skipping or intron retention; - Produces aberrant, nonfunctional mRNA and protein.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Detail the mechanism by which microRNA (miRNA) molecules silence gene expression in the cytoplasm.
back: - Guide strand associates with RISC complex; - Hybridizes with 3-prime UTR of target mRNA; - Leads to translational repression; - Triggers mRNA degradation if complementarity is high.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distinguish between cis-acting elements and trans-acting factors in gene regulation.
back: - Cis-acting: DNA sequences (e.g. TATA box) on the same chromosome; - Trans-acting: Diffusible molecules (e.g. transcription factors); - Factors transit from synthesis site to DNA target.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the enzyme class responsible for neutralizing positive charges on histones to relax chromatin structure.
back: - Histone Acetyltransferases (HATs); - Acetylate lysine residues at N-terminus; - Decreases histone-DNA affinity; - Promotes gene transcription access.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In the eukaryotic promoter, the highly conserved consensus sequence located approximately 25 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site is the [___].
back:
• TATA box (Hogness box).
• Serves as the primary binding site for General Transcription Factors (GTFs).
• Crucial for the precise positioning of RNA Polymerase II.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A biopsy reveals that the tropomyosin protein in cardiac muscle differs significantly from that in smooth muscle, despite originating from the same gene. Identify the regulatory process responsible.
back:
• Alternative Splicing.
• Involves selective inclusion or exclusion of exons from pre-mRNA.
• Enables a single gene to produce multiple tissue-specific protein isoforms.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain the role of allolactose in the regulation of the bacterial lac operon.
back:
• Acts as an inducer.
• Binds to the repressor protein, causing a conformational change.
• Prevents the repressor from binding to the operator, allowing transcription.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the structural and functional features of euchromatin with those of heterochromatin.
back:
• Euchromatin: Decondensed, transcriptionally active, and contains acetylated histones.
• Heterochromatin: Highly condensed, transcriptionally inactive, and often hypermethylated.
• Euchromatin allows DNA access; heterochromatin sequesters it.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: How does histone acetylation by Histone Acetyltransferases (HATs) facilitate gene expression?
back:
• Neutralizes the positive charge on lysine residues.
• Decreases the electrostatic attraction between histones and DNA.
• Relaxes nucleosome structure to allow transcription factor access.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distant DNA sequences that increase the rate of transcription by looping DNA to interact with the promoter complex are known as [___].
back:
• Enhancers.
• Bind specific transcription factors (activators).
• Function independently of their orientation or exact distance from the gene.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A patient is found to have abnormal gene silencing on the X chromosome due to excessive cytosine modification. Name the biochemical process involved.
back:
• DNA Methylation.
• Occurs at CpG islands in the promoter region.
• Heritable modification (epigenetics) that generally suppresses transcription.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the mechanism of attenuation in the prokaryotic tryptophan (trp) operon when tryptophan levels are high.
back:
• Rapid translation of the leader sequence occurs.
• Favors formation of a 3-4 stem-loop (attenuator).
• Triggers premature rho-independent termination of transcription.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distinguish between cis-acting and trans-acting elements in the context of gene regulation.
back:
• Cis-acting: DNA sequences (promoters/enhancers) on the same chromosome as the gene.
• Trans-acting: Diffusible molecules (transcription factors/repressors) produced by other genes.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: State the mechanism by which microRNAs (miRNAs) regulate eukaryotic gene expression post-transcriptionally.
back:
• Assemble into the RISC complex.
• Bind to the 3'-UTR of target mRNA.
• Mediate gene silencing via mRNA degradation or translational repression.

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: The non-coding sequences within a eukaryotic gene that are initially transcribed into pre-mRNA but removed during the process of splicing are called [___].
back:
* Introns
* Intervening sequences removed by spliceosomes
* Exons are the coding sequences that remain
* Essential for generating mature, functional mRNA transcripts

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A child presents with severe anemia and is diagnosed with ̢-thalassemia. Genetic testing shows a mutation at a conserved splice site. Explain the molecular effect on gene expression.
back:
* Defective RNA splicing
* Introns may be retained or exons skipped
* Produces a non-functional or truncated protein
* Leads to deficiency of functional hemoglobin chains

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain the role of DNA looping and mediator proteins in the regulation of eukaryotic gene transcription by distal enhancers.
back:
* Enhancers bind specific transcription factors
* DNA loops to bring distal enhancers near promoters
* Mediator complex bridges enhancers and the transcription complex
* Stabilizes RNA polymerase II at the start site

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A laboratory analysis of a patient's skin fibroblasts identifies regions of DNA that are hypermethylated and resistant to nuclease digestion. Contrast this finding with transcriptionally active DNA.
back:
* Hypermethylated DNA represents Heterochromatin; inactive and condensed
* Active DNA is Euchromatin; decondensed and acetylated
* Heterochromatin restricts access to RNA polymerase
* Euchromatin allows high levels of gene expression

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the specific biochemical step by which allolactose functions as an inducer for the bacterial lac operon.
back:
* Allolactose binds to the lac repressor protein
* Induces a conformational change in the repressor
* Repressor dissociates from the operator site
* Allows RNA polymerase to proceed with transcription

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Eukaryotic transcription factors are modular proteins that typically possess a [___] domain to identify specific DNA sequences and an activation domain to recruit coactivators.
back:
* DNA-binding (DBD)
* Recognizes cis-acting elements like enhancers or promoters
* Common motifs include zinc fingers and leucine zippers
* Essential for site-specific regulation of gene expression

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A patient with hereditary amyloidosis is treated with patisiran, a drug that utilizes microRNA-like mechanisms. Describe the pathophysiology of gene silencing involved in this therapy.
back:
* siRNA associates with the RISC complex
* Guide strand binds to target mRNA complementary sequences
* RISC mediates mRNA cleavage or blocks translation
* Reduces the production of the toxic amyloid protein

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism of transcriptional attenuation in the bacterial trp operon when tryptophan levels are abundant.
back:
* Rapid translation of the leader peptide occurs
* Ribosome covers sequences preventing anti-terminator loop formation
* A rho-independent terminator (hairpin) structure forms
* RNA polymerase dissociates before transcribing structural genes

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the regulation of Transferrin receptor (TfR) mRNA stability with Ferritin mRNA translation when intracellular iron levels are low.
back:
* TfR mRNA: Iron Regulatory Proteins (IRPs) bind 3'-IRE, stabilizing mRNA for translation
* Ferritin mRNA: IRPs bind 5'-IRE, blocking translation to prevent storage
* Coordinated response increases iron uptake while decreasing storage

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the specific proteins that constitute the octameric core around which DNA is wrapped to form a nucleosome.
back:
* Two molecules each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
* Basic proteins that neutralize negative DNA charge
* H1 acts as the linker histone externally
* Foundational unit of eukaryotic chromatin organization

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In eukaryotic gene expression, the [___] box is a highly conserved consensus sequence located approximately 25 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site that facilitates the assembly of the preinitiation complex.
back:
* TATA (Hogness) box
* Serves as a binding site for TFIID
* Essential for positioning RNA Polymerase II
* Crucial for initiating basal-level transcription

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: A researcher observes that a specific protein in the liver (Apo B-100) is longer than its counterpart in the intestine (Apo B-48), despite being derived from the same gene. Identify the post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism responsible for this.
back:
* RNA Editing
* Cytosine is deaminated to Uracil in the intestine
* Creates a premature stop codon (UAA)
* Results in a truncated protein specifically in intestinal cells

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism by which histone acetylation facilitates gene expression.
back:
* Acetylation by Histone Acetyltransferases (HATs) removes positive charges from lysine residues
* Weakens interaction between basic histones and acidic DNA
* Promotes chromatin decondensation (Euchromatin formation)
* Increases accessibility for transcription factors

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Contrast the genomic organization of a prokaryotic polycistronic mRNA with a eukaryotic monocistronic mRNA.
back:
* Polycistronic: One transcript containing multiple translation start/stop sites
* Monocistronic: One transcript for a single gene product
* Facilitates simultaneous synthesis of metabolic pathway enzymes in bacteria

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain the role of the 'Inducer' molecule in the negative regulation of the bacterial Lac Operon.
back:
* Allolactose binds to the repressor protein
* Induces a conformational change preventing repressor-operator binding
* Removes the physical block on RNA Polymerase
* Allows transcription of structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA)

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: The regulatory process in the tryptophan operon where transcription is prematurely terminated before the structural genes are reached, based on the speed of the trailing ribosome, is called [___].
back:
* Attenuation
* Driven by the formation of a GC-rich hairpin structure
* Couples translation directly with transcription
* Highly dependent on intracellular levels of Tryptophanyl-tRNA

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: In a patient with iron-deficiency anemia, cellular levels of the transferrin receptor increase. Explain the role of Iron Regulatory Proteins (IRPs) in this post-transcriptional regulation.
back:
* IRPs bind to Iron Responsive Elements (IREs) in the 3'-UTR
* Binding stabilizes the transferrin receptor mRNA
* Prevents endonuclease-mediated degradation
* Increases mRNA half-life, allowing for more protein synthesis

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Explain how MicroRNAs (miRNA) mediate gene silencing via the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC).
back:
* miRNA guide strand hybridizes with target mRNA's 3'-UTR
* Perfect complementarity leads to mRNA cleavage by Argonaute
* Partial complementarity results in translational repression
* Effectively reduces the expression of specific gene sets

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Distinguish between the functional roles of 'Enhancers' and 'Silencers' in eukaryotic transcription.
back:
* Enhancers: Bind activators to increase initiation frequency
* Silencers: Bind repressors to decrease gene expression
* Both act over long distances and are orientation-independent

category: Discuss the structures of genes, how they are organized and regulated
front: Identify the primary site and specific enzyme responsible for the 'Stringent Response' in bacteria during amino acid starvation.
back:
* Triggered at the ribosomal A-site by uncharged tRNA
* Enzyme: Stringent Factor (RelA)
* Produces the alarmone ppGpp
* Selectively inhibits rRNA and tRNA synthesis to conserve energy

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to Mendel’s Law of Segregation, the two [___] for a specific trait separate from each other during the formation of gametes.
back:
* Alleles
* Occurs during Meiosis (Anaphase I/II)
* Ensures each gamete carries only one copy of a gene

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple are both asymptomatic carriers for Phenylketonuria (Autosomal Recessive). Explain the genetic principle allowing them to have an affected (homozygous) child.
back:
* Law of Segregation
* Alleles 'A' and 'a' separate during meiosis
* Random fusion of two 'a' gametes creates the 'aa' genotype

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the meiotic basis for the Law of Independent Assortment during Metaphase I.
back:
* Random orientation of bivalents
* Homologous pairs align independently on the equatorial plate
* Maternal/paternal chromosomes distribute randomly to poles

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the inheritance of genes that follow Mendel's Second Law with those that exhibit genetic 'Linkage'.
back:
* Independent Assortment: Genes on different chromosomes segregate freely
* Linkage: Genes on the same chromosome inherited together
* Recombination: Crossing over can break linkage

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Specify the meiotic event that is the physical manifestation of the Law of Segregation.
back:
* Separation of homologous chromosomes
* Occurs during Anaphase I
* Followed by sister chromatid separation in Anaphase II

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Law of Independent Assortment is most accurately observed in a [___] cross, resulting in a classic 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.
back:
* Dihybrid
* Involves two different genes/traits
* Assumes genes are on non-homologous chromosomes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A patient has a dominant disorder (Aa). Using the Law of Segregation, predict the probability of passing the mutant allele to their offspring.
back:
* 50% (0.5)
* Only one allele (A or a) enters a gamete
* Random fertilization determines the final zygote genotype

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe how the 'Purity of Gametes' concept relates to Mendel's First Law.
back:
* Gametes are haploid
* They contain only one allele for any given gene
* Ensures the diploid state is restored upon fertilization

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the Law of Segregation and the Law of Independent Assortment based on the number of loci involved.
back:
* Segregation: Involves a single gene locus
* Independent Assortment: Involves two or more gene loci
* Both occur during Meiosis I

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the chromosomal condition that must be met for two genes to obey the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
* Located on different chromosomes
* OR located very far apart on the same chromosome
* Allows for frequent recombination

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to the Mendelian Law of Segregation, the two [___] for a specific gene pair separate during gametogenesis so that each gamete receives only one.
back:
• Alleles
• Occurs during Meiosis I (Anaphase I)
• Restores diploidy upon fertilization
• Explains the 3:1 phenotypic ratio

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple are both carriers for phenylketonuria (PKU). The probability that their child will inherit two recessive alleles and manifest the disease is explained by the Law of [___].
back:
• Segregation
• Alleles separate into individual gametes
• Probability calculated via Punnett square
• Standard autosomal recessive inheritance

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the chromosomal mechanism during meiosis that provides the physical basis for the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
• Random orientation of homologous pairs
• Occurs at the metaphase plate (Metaphase I)
• Distribution of one pair is unaffected by others
• Occurs only for genes on different chromosomes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the inheritance of alleles at a single gene locus with the inheritance of alleles across two different, unlinked gene loci.
back:
• Single locus: Law of Segregation (alleles separate)
• Two loci: Independent Assortment (genes shuffle)
• Segregation involves one chromosome pair
• Assortment involves multiple non-homologous pairs

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the specific meiotic stage where homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles, ensuring the Law of Segregation is fulfilled.
back:
• Anaphase I
• Separation of maternal and paternal homologs
• Sister chromatids remain attached
• Results in haploid daughter cells

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Law of Independent Assortment predicts a specific phenotypic ratio of [___] in the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross involving unlinked autosomal traits.
back:
• 9:3:3:1
• Represents four distinct phenotypic combinations
• Assumes complete dominance for both traits
• Validated by random gamete fusion

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A patient inherits a mutation for polydactyly and a separate mutation for Albinism. The observation that these traits do not consistently appear together in the patient's siblings demonstrates which Mendelian law?
back:
• Law of Independent Assortment
• Genes for different traits segregate independently
• Traits are located on different chromosomes
• Facilitates genetic recombination

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the biological necessity of the Law of Segregation regarding the maintenance of a constant species chromosome number.
back:
• Prevents doubling of chromosomes every generation
• Ensures gametes are haploid (n)
• Fusion of two haploid gametes restores diploidy (2n)
• Vital for sexual reproduction

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the behavior of linked genes and genes that follow the Law of Independent Assortment during meiosis.
back:
• Independent Assortment: Genes on different chromosomes
• Linked Genes: Located on the same chromosome
• Linked genes tend to be inherited together
• Breaking linkage requires chromosomal crossover

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Name the specific genetic term for an individual possessing two different alleles for a single trait as a result of Mendelian segregation.
back:
• Heterozygote
• Results from inheriting different paternal/maternal alleles
• Genotype usually expressed as "Aa"
• Often carries a silent recessive allele

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to the Mendelian Law of Segregation, the two [___] for a specific trait separate during gamete formation, ensuring each gamete receives only one copy.
back: * Alleles; * Occurs during meiosis; * Ensures each gamete is haploid for that specific trait.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple, both carriers for an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder, has a child. Explain which Mendelian law accounts for the child's 25% probability of being affected.
back: * Law of Segregation; * Alleles of the carrier parents separate into different gametes; * Random fusion during fertilization allows recessive alleles to pair.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the cellular mechanism that carries out the Law of Segregation during the process of meiosis.
back: * Homologous chromosomes separate during Anaphase I; * Sister chromatids separate during Anaphase II; * Results in gametes with one allele per locus.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the focus of the Law of Segregation with the focus of the Law of Independent Assortment.
back: * Segregation: Describes behavior of alleles at a single gene locus; * Independent Assortment: Describes simultaneous inheritance of multiple independent genes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the specific chromosomal requirement for two distinct genes to follow the Law of Independent Assortment.
back: * Genes must be on different chromosomes; * Alternatively, genes must be very far apart on the same chromosome to allow frequent crossing over.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The random orientation of homologous chromosome pairs at the metaphase plate during Meiosis I is the physical basis for the Law of [___].
back: * Independent Assortment; * Ensures maternal and paternal homologs distribute randomly to daughter cells; * Increases genetic diversity.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A researcher performs a dihybrid cross between two individuals heterozygous for two unlinked traits (AaBb x AaBb). Which Mendelian law explains the 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio observed?
back: * Law of Independent Assortment; * Assumes alleles for different traits distribute to gametes regardless of one another; * Predicts four distinct gamete types.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the specific stage of Meiosis I where the Law of Independent Assortment is executed and how it occurs.
back: * Metaphase I and Anaphase I; * Bivalents align randomly at the equator; * Paternal and maternal homologs segregate to poles independently of other pairs.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the expected inheritance outcomes of genes that show linkage versus those that follow Independent Assortment.
back: * Linkage: Genes are close on the same chromosome and inherited together; * Independent Assortment: Genes distribute randomly, yielding 50% recombinant frequency.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: State the mathematical formula used to calculate the number of unique gamete genotypes possible via independent assortment, where 'n' is the number of heterozygous pairs.
back: * 2^n; * 'n' represents the number of haploid heterozygous loci; * Illustrates the massive potential for genetic recombination.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian principle stating that during gamete formation, the two [___] for a single heritable character separate so that each gamete carries only one is the Law of Segregation.
back:
• Alleles
• Each gamete receives one member of the pair
• Occurs during Meiosis I

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple, both phenotypically normal, has a child with Phenylketonuria (autosomal recessive). According to the Law of Segregation, determine the expected fraction of their offspring that will be carriers (heterozygous).
back:
• 1/2 (one-half)
• Each parent is a carrier (Aa)
• Probability calculation: 2/4 based on monohybrid cross

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the biological requirement for the Law of Independent Assortment to apply to two different gene loci.
back:
• Genes must be located on different chromosomes
• Or be located very far apart on the same chromosome
• Prevents genetic linkage from interfering with random distribution

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the number of gene pairs involved.
back:
• Law of Segregation: Applies to a single gene pair (one locus)
• Law of Independent Assortment: Applies to two or more gene pairs (multiple loci)
• Segregation describes allele separation; Independent Assortment describes how different genes distribute

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the classic genotypic ratio resulting from an F1 monohybrid cross between two heterozygous (Aa) individuals.
back:
• 1:2:1
• 1 Homozygous Dominant (AA)
• 2 Heterozygous (Aa)
• 1 Homozygous Recessive (aa)

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: In clinical genetics, the physical location of a specific gene on its respective chromosome is referred to as the [___].
back:
• Locus
• Plural is 'loci'
• Essential for determining linkage and independent assortment

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A patient with Huntington’s Disease (autosomal dominant) is heterozygous. Their spouse has a normal genotype. Predict the fraction of their children expected to exhibit the phenotype.
back:
• 1/2 (one-half)
• Follows the Law of Segregation
• Affected parent (Hh) passes the dominant allele to half of the gametes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the specific event in Meiosis I that provides the physical basis for the Law of Segregation.
back:
• Separation of homologous chromosomes
• Occurs during Anaphase I
• Ensures each daughter cell receives only one allele from the original pair

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the phenotypic and genotypic outcomes of a Mendelian monohybrid cross involving a trait with complete dominance.
back:
• Genotypic Ratio: 1:2:1 (AA:Aa:aa)
• Phenotypic Ratio: 3:1 (Dominant:Recessive)
• Heterozygotes (Aa) are phenotypically identical to homozygous dominant (AA)

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the expected F2 phenotypic ratio for a dihybrid cross assuming both gene pairs follow the Law of Independent Assortment and show complete dominance.
back:
• 9:3:3:1
• Represents the random combination of two 3:1 monohybrid ratios
• Assumes genes are on non-homologous chromosomes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to the Law of Segregation, during the process of gamete formation, the two [___] for a specific gene separate so that each gamete carries only one.
back:
- Alleles.
- Ensures offspring receive one hereditary factor from each parent.
- Occurs during Anaphase I of meiosis.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple, both carriers for a recessive metabolic disorder, has a child with the disease. Identify the Mendelian principle explaining how healthy parents can produce an affected child.
back:
- Law of Segregation.
- Heterozygous parents (Aa) produce gametes with either 'A' or 'a'.
- Fusion of two 'a' gametes results in an 'aa' affected phenotype.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the cellular mechanism occurring during Metaphase I of meiosis that facilitates the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
- Random orientation of homologous pairs at the metaphase plate.
- Paternal and maternal chromosomes align independently of other pairs.
- Leads to diverse combinations of maternal/paternal alleles in gametes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the dihybrid phenotypic ratios seen in genes following the Law of Independent Assortment with those involving complete genetic linkage.
back:
- Independent Assortment: Produces a 9:3:3:1 ratio in F2 generation.
- Complete Linkage: Mimics a monohybrid cross (3:1 ratio).
- Linked genes do not separate independently during meiosis.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Name the statistical tool used to predict the genetic outcomes of Independent Assortment for a cross between two dihybrid individuals (AaBb x AaBb).
back:
- Punnett Square.
- Predicts 16 possible allele combinations.
- Results in four distinct phenotypes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian principle stating that alleles of different genes are distributed to gametes without influencing one another is the Law of [___].
back:
- Independent Assortment.
- Applies primarily to genes on different chromosomes or distant loci.
- Increases genetic variation via chromosomal shuffling.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A patient with Type O blood has parents with Type A and Type B blood. Apply the Law of Segregation to explain the parents' genotypes.
back:
- Both parents must be heterozygous (AO and BO).
- Each parent segregated the 'O' allele into their gametes.
- The zygote received one 'O' from each parent, resulting in OO.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe how the physical distance between two loci on the same chromosome affects their ability to comply with the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
- Distant loci are likely separated by crossing over (recombination).
- Distances ≥50 cM allow independent assortment despite being on one chromosome.
- Proximal loci remain linked, violating independent assortment expectations.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the Law of Segregation and the Law of Independent Assortment based on the meiotic stage in which they originate.
back:
- Independent Assortment: Originates in Metaphase I (random alignment).
- Segregation: Originates in Anaphase I (physical separation of homologs).
- Both contribute to unique genetic profiles in haploid cells.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: State the number of alleles for a single autosomal gene found in a mature human sperm cell according to Mendelian principles.
back:
- One allele.
- Gametes are haploid (n) due to segregation.
- Restores the diploid number (2n) upon fertilization with an egg.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to the [___], the two alleles for a single genetic locus separate during meiosis so that each gamete carries only one allele for that specific trait.
back:
Law of Segregation.
- Occurs during Anaphase I of meiosis.
- Ensures offspring receive one allele from each parent.
- Explains the 3:1 phenotypic ratio in monohybrid crosses.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A man is a carrier for Albinism (autosomal recessive). According to Mendel's first law, the physiological process ensuring that 50% of his sperm carry the recessive allele is the [___].
back:
Law of Segregation.
- Results from separation of homologous chromosomes.
- Restores the diploid number upon fertilization.
- Prevents gametes from possessing multiple alleles for one gene.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the meiotic mechanism that allows the alleles of two different genes to be distributed into gametes without influencing one another.
back:
Law of Independent Assortment.
- Random alignment of non-homologous pairs in Metaphase I.
- Maternal and paternal chromosomes shuffle independently.
- Leads to genetic variation in gametes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the number of gene pairs involved in each principle.
back:
Segregation:
- Concerns the separation of a single pair of alleles (one gene).
Independent Assortment:
- Concerns the simultaneous inheritance of two or more different gene pairs.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the specific genomic condition where two genes fail to follow the Law of Independent Assortment despite being on the same chromosome.
back:
Genetic Linkage.
- Occurs when loci are physically close.
- Reduces independent shuffling during meiosis.
- Frequency of recombination is less than 50%.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The biological principle stating that the inheritance of one trait, like hair color, has no effect on the inheritance of another, like height, is known as the Law of [___].
back:
Independent Assortment.
- Applies only to genes on separate chromosomes.
- Also applies to genes very far apart on one chromosome.
- Demonstrated by 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratios.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A child inherits an autosomal dominant disorder from her father and a separate autosomal recessive trait from her mother. The fact that these two traits do not always appear together in siblings is an application of [___].
back:
Law of Independent Assortment.
- Assumes genes are on different chromosomes.
- Each trait is inherited as a distinct unit.
- Explains diversity among siblings with the same parents.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the significance of the 3:1 phenotypic ratio observed in the F2 generation of a monohybrid cross in the context of Mendel's laws.
back:
- Supports the Law of Segregation.
- Proves alleles are discrete units (not blended).
- Demonstrates that recessive traits can reappear when paired.
- 1:2:1 genotypic ratio underlies the 3:1 phenotype.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the Law of Segregation and the Law of Independent Assortment based on their respective stages in the meiotic cycle.
back:
Segregation:
- Primarily Anaphase I (separation of homologs).
Independent Assortment:
- Primarily Metaphase I (random equatorial alignment).

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Which Mendelian law explains why a gamete produced by a heterozygous (Aa) individual is 'pure' for either the 'A' or 'a' allele?
back:
Law of Segregation.
- Also known as the 'Law of Purity of Gametes'.
- Ensures each gamete is haploid.
- Prevents mixing of dominant and recessive information.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian Law of [___] states that during gamete formation, the two alleles for a heritable character separate such that each gamete receives only one allele.
back:
• Law of Segregation
• Occurs during Meiosis I
• Ensures each gamete is haploid for that specific gene locus

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple, both carriers for an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder, has a 25% chance of having an affected child. This predictability of individual allele inheritance is based on the Law of [___].
back:
• Law of Segregation
• Explains why offspring can display phenotypes absent in parents
• Forms the basis of Punnett square calculations for single traits

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the role of Meiosis I in fulfilling the Mendelian Law of Segregation.
back:
• Homologous chromosomes separate during Anaphase I
• Alleles located at the same locus on homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles
• Results in gametes containing only one allele per gene

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Mendelian Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the number of gene loci involved.
back:
• Segregation: Pertains to alleles at a single gene locus
• Independent Assortment: Pertains to the relationship between two or more different gene loci
• Segregation occurs regardless of linkage; Independent Assortment requires genes on different chromosomes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Under what specific chromosomal condition is the Mendelian Law of Independent Assortment typically violated?
back:
• Genetic Linkage
• Occurs when genes are located close together on the same chromosome
• These genes tend to be inherited together unless crossing over occurs

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian Law of [___] posits that the alleles of one gene pair sort into gametes without being influenced by the sorting of alleles for another gene pair.
back:
• Law of Independent Assortment
• Applies to genes located on different (non-homologous) chromosomes
• Increases genetic variation in offspring

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A pedigree analysis shows that the inheritance of Albinism (autosomal recessive) does not correlate with the inheritance of ABO blood groups. Identify the Mendelian principle demonstrated.
back:
• Law of Independent Assortment
• Different traits on different chromosomes segregate independently
• Produces a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in a dihybrid cross

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: How does the alignment of chromosomes during Metaphase I of Meiosis provide the mechanism for Independent Assortment?
back:
• Random orientation of homologous pairs at the metaphase plate
• The direction a maternal chromosome faces is independent of other pairs
• Leads to 2^n possible chromosomal combinations in gametes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the phenotypic ratios produced by a monohybrid cross versus a dihybrid cross involving completely dominant Mendelian traits.
back:
• Monohybrid (Law of Segregation): 3:1 ratio
• Dihybrid (Law of Independent Assortment): 9:3:3:1 ratio
• Assumes both parents are heterozygous for all involved traits

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the primary biological consequence of Mendelian Independent Assortment for human populations.
back:
• Genetic Recombination/Diversity
• Creation of new combinations of alleles in gametes
• Essential for evolutionary adaptation and survival

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to the Mendelian Law of [___], the two alleles for a heritable character separate from each other during gamete formation and end up in different gametes.
back:
• Segregation
• Occurs during Anaphase I of meiosis
• Ensures each gamete receives only one allele per locus
• Results in the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio in monohybrid crosses

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A researcher crosses two plants heterozygous for a single trait (Aa x Aa). The offspring show a 3:1 phenotypic ratio. This outcome provides evidence for which Mendelian principle?
back:
• Law of Segregation
• Demonstrates that alleles of a single gene behave as discrete units
• Particulate inheritance replaces 'blending' theories
• Requires separation of homologous chromosomes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the molecular mechanism during meiosis that provides the physical basis for Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
• Random orientation of homologous pairs
• Occurs during Metaphase I
• Alignment of one pair is independent of other pairs
• Produces 2^n possible chromosomal combinations in gametes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the number of gene loci involved in the cross.
back:
• Segregation: Involves a single locus (one gene pair)
• Independent Assortment: Involves two or more loci (different gene pairs)
• Segregation applies to all alleles; Independent Assortment applies only to unlinked genes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the specific stage of meiosis where the physical separation of homologous chromosomes ensures that each gamete carries only one allele for a specific gene.
back:
• Anaphase I
• Sister chromatids remain attached at this stage
• Homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles
• Defines the Law of Segregation

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Law of Independent Assortment is most typically demonstrated using a [___] cross, which tracks the inheritance of two different characters simultaneously.
back:
• Dihybrid cross
• Yields a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation
• Assumes alleles are located on different chromosomes
• Illustrates trait-independent shuffling

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: In a study of two human traits (A and B), it is observed that the inheritance of trait A has no influence on the probability of inheriting trait B. Name this principle and its primary requirement.
back:
• Law of Independent Assortment
• Requirement: Genes must be on non-homologous chromosomes (unlinked)
• Also possible if genes are very far apart on the same chromosome

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe how the process of meiosis produces the 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio observed in Mendel's classic dihybrid experiments.
back:
• Independent alignment of tetrads at the metaphase plate
• Random combination of four gamete types (e.g., AB, Ab, aB, ab)
• Equal probability (25%) for each gametic combination
• Results in 16 possible zygotic outcomes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the expected phenotypic ratios of a monohybrid cross versus a dihybrid cross involving two parents heterozygous for all traits.
back:
• Monohybrid (Aa x Aa): 3:1 ratio
• Dihybrid (AaBb x AaBb): 9:3:3:1 ratio
• The dihybrid ratio is mathematically (3:1) x (3:1)
• Confirms independent inheritance patterns

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: State the primary genetic phenomenon that serves as the major exception to Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
• Genetic Linkage
• Occurs when genes are physically close on the same chromosome
• Segregate together more often than expected by chance
• Frequency of recombination depends on the distance between loci

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian principle stating that the two alleles of a single gene locus separate from each other during gamete formation is the Law of [___].
back:
Law of Segregation.
- Occurs during Anaphase I of meiosis.
- Ensures each gamete carries only one allele per locus.
- Restores diploid status upon fertilization.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A child is born with albinism (autosomal recessive) to two phenotypically normal parents. Identify the Mendelian law that explains why this recessive trait was hidden in the parents but reappeared in the offspring.
back:
Law of Segregation.
- Parents are heterozygous carriers.
- Recessive alleles separate during gametogenesis.
- Zygote receives one recessive allele from each parent, manifesting the phenotype.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the mechanical role of homologous chromosome separation during Meiosis I in fulfilling Mendel's First Law.
back:
Physical Disjunction.
- Homologous pairs align and separate to opposite poles.
- This prevents gametes from receiving two copies of the same gene.
- Results in the 1:1 ratio of alleles in a population of gametes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A researcher performs a dihybrid cross for two traits and observes a 9:3:1 phenotypic ratio. Analyze why this outcome would change if the two gene loci were located very close to each other on the same chromosome.
back:
Genetic Linkage.
- Linked genes do not assort independently.
- Offspring would show higher frequency of parental phenotypes.
- Violates Mendel’s Law of Independent Assortment due to lack of crossing over.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Define the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the relationship between different pairs of alleles.
back:
Random Distribution.
- Alleles for one trait segregate independently of alleles for another trait.
- Only applies to genes on different chromosomes.
- Essential for creating genetic variation in gametes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The physical basis for the Law of Independent Assortment is the random orientation of [___] at the metaphase plate during Meiosis I.
back:
Homologous Chromosome Pairs.
- Random alignment in Metaphase I leads to various paternal/maternal combinations.
- Each pair assorts without influence from others.
- Generates 2^n possible gametic combinations.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple has a child with both Cystic Fibrosis (autosomal recessive) and Polydactyly (autosomal dominant). If these genes are on different chromosomes, apply Mendelian principles to predict the risk of the next child having both conditions compared to just one.
back:
Independent Probability.
- Risk of inheriting one trait is independent of the other.
- Total risk is calculated by multiplying individual probabilities.
- Follows the 9:3:1 dihybrid ratio in a heterozygous cross.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the specific meiotic error that leads to a failure of the Law of Segregation and name the typical clinical result.
back:
Non-disjunction.
- Failure of homologs or sister chromatids to separate.
- Results in gametes with extra or missing chromosomes.
- Clinically manifests as aneuploidy syndromes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment based on the number of gene loci involved in each process.
back:
Loci Comparison.
- Segregation: Involves one gene locus and its two alleles.
- Independent Assortment: Involves at least two different gene loci.
- Segregation occurs in all sexual reproduction; Assortment requires multiple traits.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the primary phase of meiosis where the physical segregation of alleles occurs to ensure haploid gametes.
back:
Anaphase I.
- Homologous chromosomes are pulled to opposite poles.
- This is the moment alleles at a locus physically separate.
- Crucial for preventing polyploidy in offspring.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian law stating that the two alleles for a heritable character separate during gamete formation and end up in different gametes is the Law of [___].
back:
*   Law of Segregation.
*   Ensures each gamete receives only one allele.
*   Physical basis occurs during Anaphase I of meiosis.
*   Results in a 3:1 phenotypic ratio in monohybrid crosses.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
coreConcept: Law of Segregation in Recessive Disorders
front: A child is born with Albinism (autosomal recessive) to two parents with normal skin pigmentation. Explain the genetic mechanism based on Mendel's first law.
back:
*   Parents are carriers (Heterozygous, Aa).
*   Law of Segregation: Alleles 'A' and 'a' separate during gamete formation.
*   Recessive phenotype 'aa' reappears when two 'a' gametes fuse.
*   Probability for this occurrence is 25%.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the specific meiotic event that serves as the biological basis for the Law of Segregation.
back:
*   Separation of homologous chromosomes.
*   Occurs during Anaphase I.
*   Ensures gametes transition from diploid (2n) to haploid (n).
*   Each gamete contains only one member of an allelic pair.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A clinician compares a family with Sickle Cell Trait (single gene) to one with Hypertension (polygenic). Contrast the segregation of the HbS allele with the inheritance of multiple blood pressure genes.
back:
*   HbS Segregation: Single-locus alleles separate into different gametes independently.
*   Polygenic Inheritance: Multiple genes at different loci assort to influence one trait.
*   HbS follows discrete 3:1 ratios; Hypertension shows continuous variation.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Determine the expected phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross where both traits follow the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
*   9:3:3:1 ratio.
*   9 (both dominant), 1 (both recessive).
*   3 and 3 (recombinant phenotypes).
*   Requires genes to be on non-homologous chromosomes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian principle stating that the inheritance of one pair of alleles is entirely unaffected by the inheritance of a second pair is the Law of [___].
back:
*   Law of Independent Assortment.
*   Applies only to genes on different chromosomes (or far apart).
*   Promotes genetic variation through new combinations.
*   Observed during Metaphase I of meiosis.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Two distinct clinical traits are found to be inherited together in 95% of cases in a large pedigree. Identify the genetic phenomenon that violates the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
*   Genetic Linkage.
*   Genes are located close together on the same chromosome.
*   They tend to be inherited as a single unit.
*   Only 'crossing over' can separate linked genes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the mechanical difference between chromosomal behavior in Anaphase I versus the random orientation in Metaphase I regarding Mendel's laws.
back:
*   Anaphase I (Segregation): Homologs separate, ensuring one allele per gamete.
*   Metaphase I (Independent Assortment): Pairs align randomly at the equator.
*   Random alignment determines which combination of non-homologous chromosomes enters a gamete.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the genotypic and phenotypic ratios observed in the offspring of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Aa x Aa).
back:
*   Genotypic Ratio: 1:2:1 (1 AA, 2 Aa, 1 aa).
*   Phenotypic Ratio: 3:1 (3 Dominant, 1 Recessive).
