*   Difference arises because heterozygotes (Aa) express the dominant phenotype.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the primary reason why Mendel's first law is frequently termed the 'Law of Purity of Gametes'.
back:
*   Allelic separation: Gametes never contain both alleles of a pair.
*   Each gamete is 'pure' for only one specific trait.
*   Ensures offspring receive one maternal and one paternal factor.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Mendel's Law of [___] states that the two alleles for a trait separate into individual gametes during meiosis, ensuring each germ cell carries only one copy of a specific gene.
back:
• Segregation
• Alleles for a single gene separate into different germ cells
• Explains how recessive traits can skip generations in a pedigree

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
coreConcept: Law of Segregation in Recessive Disorders
front: A phenotypically normal couple has a child with Cystic Fibrosis. This clinical example demonstrates the separation of discrete parental alleles during gamete formation, confirming the Law of [___].
back:
• Segregation
• Each parent contributes one discrete allele to the offspring
• Proves that alleles do not 'blend' but remain distinct units

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain how the movement of homologous chromosomes in Anaphase I validates the Law of Segregation.
back:
• Homologs carrying different alleles move to opposite poles
• Reduces the diploid genome to a haploid state
• Ensures gametes receive only one allele of the pair

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the number of gene loci involved.
back:
• Segregation: Focuses on the separation of alleles at a single gene locus
• Independent Assortment: Focuses on the separation of alleles of two or more different genes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Summarize the expected phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes.
back:
• 3:1 phenotypic ratio (Dominant:Recessive)
• Results from the random recombination of segregated alleles
• Genotypic ratio is 1:2:1 (AA:Aa:aa)

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Law of Independent Assortment is fundamentally rooted in the random alignment of [___] pairs during Metaphase I of meiosis.
back:
• Non-homologous chromosomes (or Bivalents)
• The orientation of one pair is independent of another
• Results in 2^n possible gametic combinations

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: An inheritance pattern shows that alleles for two distinct traits are consistently inherited together, deviating from expected random distribution. Identify the principle that limits the Law of [___].
back:
• Independent Assortment
• Limited by genetic linkage
• Genes physically close on the same chromosome tend to be inherited as a unit

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Relate the physical distance of genes on a chromosome to the probability of following the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
• Genes far apart or on different chromosomes assort independently
• Genes close together are 'linked'
• High recombination frequency allows distant genes on one chromosome to appear unlinked

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the segregation of alleles at a single locus and the assortment of alleles across multiple loci during gametogenesis.
back:
• Segregation partitions alleles of one gene into different cells
• Independent Assortment distributes alleles of multiple different gene pairs randomly relative to each other

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the specific chromosomal structure whose separation in Meiosis I is the physical basis for Mendel's first law.
back:
• Homologous chromosomes
• Their separation in Anaphase I ensures each gamete receives a single set of instructions for each trait

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, only one copy of a mutant allele is necessary for the disease phenotype to be expressed in both males and females, often showing vertical transmission.
back:
• Autosomal Dominant (AD)
• Phenotype appears in every generation
• 50% risk to offspring of an affected parent
• Equal frequency in both sexes

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child presents with chronic lung infections and pancreatic insufficiency. Both parents are clinically healthy, but the child is diagnosed with Cystic Fibrosis. Identify the characteristic inheritance pattern.
back:
• Autosomal Recessive (AR)
• Typically horizontal transmission (siblings affected)
• 25% recurrence risk for each pregnancy
• Parents are usually asymptomatic carriers

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why males are predominantly affected in X-linked recessive disorders such as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy compared to females.
back:
• Males are hemizygous for the X chromosome
• One mutant X allele causes the disease
• Females require two mutant alleles or extreme lyonization
• Male-to-male transmission never occurs

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the inheritance of an X-linked dominant trait from an affected father with an autosomal dominant trait regarding his daughters.
back:
• X-linked Dominant: 100% of daughters are affected (receive paternal X).
• Autosomal Dominant: 50% risk for daughters.
• X-linked Dominant: 0% of sons are affected by the father.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the transmission pattern of mitochondrial DNA mutations from an affected father to his offspring.
back:
• 0% transmission (Maternal inheritance only)
• Mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the oocyte
• Affected females pass the trait to all children
• Shows heteroplasmy (variable expressivity)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Hemophilia A, characterized by Factor VIII deficiency and prolonged bleeding, follows an [___] inheritance pattern.
back:
• X-linked Recessive
• Primarily affects males
• Transmitted by carrier females
• "Knight’s move" skip-generation pattern in pedigrees

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 40-year-old male presents with diabetes and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. His mother and two sisters are similarly affected, but his children are all healthy. Identify the most likely inheritance.
back:
• Mitochondrial Inheritance
• Maternal inheritance pattern (mother to all children)
• Affected males do not transmit to offspring
• Affects high-energy organs (pancreas, CNS)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the significance of "Vertical Transmission" in the pedigree of Huntington’s Disease.
back:
• Phenotype appears in every generation without skipping
• Every affected individual has an affected parent
• Hallmarks of Autosomal Dominant traits
• Equal sex distribution observed

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between Autosomal Recessive and X-linked Recessive patterns in a pedigree lacking consanguinity.
back:
• Autosomal Recessive: Equal male/female ratio; horizontal siblings affected.
• X-linked Recessive: Strong male bias; females are carriers.
• X-linked: No male-to-male transmission.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern of Vitamin D resistant rickets where an affected female has a 50% chance of passing the trait to both sons and daughters.
back:
• X-linked Dominant
• Twice as frequent in females as in males
• Affected males pass to all daughters, zero sons
• Females may show milder symptoms due to lyonization

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian Law of Segregation dictates that the two alleles for each gene separate during gamete formation, a biological process occurring specifically during [___] of meiosis.
back:
* Anaphase I.
* This ensures that each gamete (sperm or egg) receives only one of the two alleles present in the parent.
* It maintains the haploid state of gametes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple are both carriers for an autosomal recessive condition. Their offspring has a 25% chance of manifesting the disease. Explain which Mendelian law allows two phenotypically normal parents to have an affected child.
back:
* Law of Segregation.
* Each parent possesses one dominant and one recessive allele.
* During meiosis, these alleles separate into different gametes.
* Fusion of two recessive-carrying gametes produces the affected homozygous recessive phenotype.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the intracellular mechanism of chromosome alignment that provides the physical basis for the Law of Independent Assortment.
back:
* Occurs during Metaphase I of meiosis.
* Homologous pairs (tetrads) align randomly at the metaphase plate.
* The orientation of one pair is independent of other pairs, creating multiple possible combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in gametes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding their meiotic orientation and chromosomal focus.
back:
* Segregation: Focuses on the separation of alleles at a single locus during Anaphase I.
* Independent Assortment: Focuses on the random distribution of alleles for multiple, different genes during Metaphase I.
* Both contribute to genetic variation.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the genetic consequence for the offspring if the Law of Segregation fails to occur correctly during meiotic division.
back:
* Nondisjunction.
* Results in aneuploidy, where gametes receive either zero or two copies of a chromosome.
* Leads to clinical conditions like Trisomy (e.g., Down syndrome) or Monosomy (e.g., Turner syndrome).

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: While Mendel's second law suggests genes distribute into gametes without influence from others, this is violated when genes are located very close together on the same chromosome, a state called [___].
back:
* Genetic Linkage.
* Linked genes tend to be inherited as a single unit.
* Violation of the Law of Independent Assortment depends on the physical distance between loci on the chromosome.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A researcher tracks two distinct genetic traits through several generations. The traits consistently appear in a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation. Which Mendelian principle does this specific ratio confirm?
back:
* Law of Independent Assortment.
* This ratio occurs in a dihybrid cross of heterozygous individuals.
* It demonstrates that the inheritance of one trait (e.g., height) does not influence the inheritance of another (e.g., color).

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the mechanistic relationship between meiotic crossing over and the restoration of Independent Assortment for genes on the same chromosome.
back:
* Crossing over (recombination) occurs during Prophase I.
* It exchanges segments between homologous non-sister chromatids.
* This allows alleles on the same chromosome to eventually assort independently if the distance between them is sufficiently large.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the expected phenotypic ratios of a monohybrid cross versus a dihybrid cross involving two heterozygous parents under complete dominance.
back:
* Monohybrid (Segregation): 3:1 phenotypic ratio.
* Dihybrid (Independent Assortment): 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio.
* These ratios represent the mathematical probability of independent allele separation and random gametic fusion.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Specify the biological advantage provided by the Law of Independent Assortment in human populations.
back:
* Increased genetic diversity.
* It reshuffles maternal and paternal alleles into unique combinations.
* Essential for the health of a population by providing varied traits for natural selection and environmental adaptation.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian Law of [___] states that the two alleles for a single heritable character separate during gamete formation and end up in different gametes.
back:
• Law of Segregation.
• Ensures each gamete receives only one allele.
• Occurs during Meiosis I.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A couple, both carriers for Phenylketonuria (PKU), has a child with the disease. Explain the genetic principle allowing a recessive phenotype to appear from two unaffected parents.
back:
• Law of Segregation.
• Heterozygous parents (Aa) each produce 'a' gametes.
• Fusion of two 'a' gametes results in 'aa' (affected) offspring.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: How does the alignment of homologous chromosome pairs during metaphase I facilitate the Law of Independent Assortment?
back:
• Random orientation of tetrads.
• Alleles of different genes segregate into gametes independently.
• Only applies to genes on different chromosomes.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Mendelian Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the number of gene loci involved in a single cross.
back:
• Segregation: Involves alleles at a single locus.
• Independent Assortment: Involves alleles at two or more different loci.
• Segregation occurs in monohybrid; Independent Assortment in dihybrid crosses.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the critical step in the 'inheritance process' where the 3:1 phenotypic ratio is established in a monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes.
back:
• Random fertilization step.
• Fusion of gametes (A and a) from both parents.
• Results in 1AA:2Aa:1aa genotypic and 3:1 phenotypic ratios.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian Law of [___] is only valid for genes located on different chromosomes or those located far apart on the same chromosome.
back:
• Law of Independent Assortment.
• Exceptions occur due to genetic linkage.
• Physical distance reduces likelihood of recombination.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A patient inherits a mutation for Polydactyly from their father and a mutation for Cystic Fibrosis from their mother. If these genes are on different chromosomes, identify the probability of their sibling inheriting both based on Mendelian laws.
back:
• Based on Law of Independent Assortment.
• Calculation uses the Product Rule.
• Inheritance of one trait does not affect the other.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain why the physical separation of sister chromatids in Meiosis II is NOT the primary basis for the Law of Segregation, compared to the events of Meiosis I.
back:
• Segregation occurs at Meiosis I (Anaphase I).
• Homologous chromosomes (carrying different alleles) separate here.
• Meiosis II only separates identical sister chromatids (barring crossover).

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between 'Independent Assortment' and 'Linked Genes' in the context of the physical 'Inheritance Loop'.
back:
• Independent Assortment: Genes on different chromosomes; 50% recombination frequency.
• Linked Genes: Located close on the same chromosome; inherited together.
• Linkage violates Mendel's second law.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the expected phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a Mendelian dihybrid cross (RrYy x RrYy) assuming complete dominance.
back:
• 9:3:3:1 ratio.
• 9 (Double Dominant).
• 3 (Dominant/Recessive) each.
• 1 (Double Recessive).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, a single copy of a mutant allele on a non-sex chromosome is sufficient to express the phenotype, typically appearing in every generation.
back:
Autosomal Dominant inheritance:
* Vertical transmission pattern
* No skipped generations
* 50% risk for offspring of an affected parent

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 5-year-old boy presents with severe photosensitivity and skin cancers. Both parents are healthy, but they are first cousins. Identify the likely inheritance pattern.
back:
Autosomal Recessive inheritance:
* Often associated with consanguinity
* Horizontal transmission (affects siblings)
* Frequently skips generations

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the biological reason why X-linked recessive disorders like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy primarily manifest in males.
back:
Males are hemizygous:
* Possess only one X chromosome
* Lack a second X allele to mask recessive mutations
* Express the trait if the single X is mutant

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: X-linked Dominant vs. Autosomal Dominant Differentiation
front: Contrast the transmission of an X-linked dominant trait with an autosomal dominant trait when the father is the only affected parent.
back:
X-linked Dominant:
* All daughters affected; 0% sons affected
Autosomal Dominant:
* 50% chance for both sons and daughters

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the inheritance risk for the offspring of a male affected by a mitochondrial disorder (e.g., mitochondrial diabetes).
back:
Zero risk of transmission:
* Mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the oocyte
* Affected males do not pass mitochondrial traits to any children

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In autosomal recessive conditions, an individual who possesses one mutant allele and one normal allele is termed an asymptomatic [___].
back:
Heterozygote (or Carrier):
* Does not show disease phenotype
* Can pass the mutant allele to offspring

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with Huntington’s disease. Every generation in his family tree is affected. Predict the probability of his children inheriting the mutation.
back:
50% (1 in 2) probability:
* Huntington's follows Autosomal Dominant inheritance
* Only one parent needs to pass the allele

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain how the 'Law of Segregation' dictates the phenotypic ratio in the offspring of two carriers of an autosomal recessive trait.
back:
Alleles separate during gamete formation:
* 25% homozygous affected
* 50% heterozygous carriers
* 25% homozygous normal

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between X-linked recessive and X-linked dominant patterns regarding the phenotype of a heterozygous female.
back:
X-linked Recessive:
* Female is an asymptomatic carrier
X-linked Dominant:
* Female expresses the clinical disease

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the parent responsible for the transmission of mitochondrial traits to all children in a pedigree.
back:
The Mother (Maternal Line):
* Cytoplasmic inheritance via the egg
* Affects all children of an affected female

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to the Mendelian Law of Segregation, the two alleles for a heritable character separate from each other during [___] and end up in different gametes.
back:
* Gamete formation (Meiosis)
* Ensures each gamete receives only one allele
* Explains the 3:1 phenotypic ratio observed in the F2 generation

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A researcher observes that the inheritance of hair color does not influence the inheritance of height in a large pedigree. This observation specifically demonstrates the principle of [___].
back:
* Mendelian Law of Independent Assortment
* Alleles of different genes segregate independently
* Applies to genes on different chromosomes or those far apart on one chromosome

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Describe the meiotic stage and physical mechanism that provides the biological basis for Mendel's Law of Segregation.
back:
* Occurs during Anaphase I of meiosis
* Homologous chromosomes (carrying distinct alleles) move to opposite poles
* Results in haploid daughter cells containing only one allele per locus

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the Law of Segregation with the Law of Independent Assortment regarding the number of gene loci involved in the observation.
back:
* Segregation: Concerns the separation of alleles at a single locus
* Independent Assortment: Concerns the relative behavior of alleles at two or more different loci

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the specific cytological event during meiosis that dictates the "Independent Assortment" of alleles for genes located on non-homologous chromosomes.
back:
* Random orientation of homologous pairs
* Occurs at the metaphase plate during Metaphase I
* Leads to varied combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in gametes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: In a Mendelian dihybrid cross involving two heterozygous parents (AaBb x AaBb), the Law of Independent Assortment predicts a phenotypic ratio of [___].
back:
* 9:3:3:1
* Represents four distinct phenotypic combinations
* Assumes the absence of genetic linkage between the two investigated loci

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A genetic study finds that two autosomal traits are almost always inherited together, contradicting Mendel’s Second Law. Explain the likely chromosomal arrangement of these genes.
back:
* Genetic Linkage
* Genes are located very close to each other on the same chromosome
* They do not assort independently during meiotic division

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain how "Crossing Over" affects the Law of Independent Assortment for genes located on the same chromosome.
back:
* Occurs during Prophase I of meiosis
* Breaks physical linkage between genes on the same chromosome
* Allows genes far apart to appear as if they assort independently

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Distinguish between the expected F2 phenotypic outcomes of a Mendelian monohybrid cross versus a dihybrid cross.
back:
* Monohybrid: 3:1 (Dominant:Recessive phenotypic ratio)
* Dihybrid: 9:3:3:1 (Double dominant:Mixed:Mixed:Double recessive ratio)
* Both depend on complete dominance and independent allele segregation

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Name the type of cross used to determine if an individual with a dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous, thereby confirming the Law of Segregation.
back:
* Test Cross
* Crossing the unknown dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive individual
* Outcomes confirm if alleles segregated from a single or identical source

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree showing an [___] inheritance pattern, an affected individual typically has an affected parent, and there is a 50% chance of transmission to each offspring.
back: **Autosomal Dominant**. - Shows vertical transmission. - Affects both sexes with equal frequency. - Trait appears in every generation (no skipping).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child presents with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. Both parents are clinically normal but are third cousins. Identify the underlying inheritance pattern.
back: **Autosomal Recessive**. - Often associated with consanguinity. - Parents are typically asymptomatic carriers. - Risk of recurrence among siblings is 25%.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the phenotypic outcome for the daughters of a male affected by an X-linked recessive disorder, assuming the mother is homozygous normal.
back: **100% Obligate Carriers**. - Daughters inherit the father's only (affected) X chromosome. - Phenotypically normal due to a second healthy X from the mother. - None are affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the pedigree 'vertical' distribution seen in Autosomal Dominant traits with the 'horizontal' distribution of Autosomal Recessive traits.
back: **Vertical (AD)**: Trait appears in multiple consecutive generations. **Horizontal (AR)**: Trait usually limited to siblings (one generation); parents are often asymptomatic carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Specify the inheritance pattern where an affected father passes the trait to all his daughters but none of his sons.
back: **X-linked Dominant**. - Affected males pass to 100% of daughters. - Zero male-to-male transmission. - Affected females pass to 50% of both sons and daughters.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A pedigree showing all children of an affected female having the disease, while no children of an affected male are affected, indicates [___] inheritance.
back: **Mitochondrial (Maternal)**. - Transmitted exclusively through females. - High variability due to heteroplasmy. - Affects energy-demanding tissues (muscle, nerves).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A male infant is diagnosed with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy. A maternal uncle is also affected, but the father and mother are normal. Determine the inheritance pattern.
back: **X-linked Recessive**. - Primarily affects males. - Mothers are asymptomatic carriers. - 50% risk for sons of a carrier female.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why mitochondrial disorders exhibit strictly maternal inheritance despite both parents contributing genetic material to the zygote.
back: **Cytoplasmic Inheritance**. - All zygotic mitochondria originate from the oocyte. - Paternal mitochondria entering the egg are actively ubiquitinated and degraded. - Sons/daughters both inherit from the mother.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Differentiate between X-linked dominant and Autosomal dominant inheritance based on the possibility of male-to-male transmission.
back: **X-linked Dominant**: Male-to-male transmission is impossible (father gives Y to sons). **Autosomal Dominant**: Male-to-male transmission occurs frequently. This distinction is critical for pedigree analysis.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the statistical recurrence risk for a child born to two parents who are both carriers of an Autosomal Recessive trait.
back: **25% (1 in 4)**. - 25% chance of being affected. - 50% chance of being a carrier. - 25% chance of being homozygous normal.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, the trait typically appears in every generation (vertical transmission), and each child of an affected parent has a 50% probability of inheriting the phenotype.
back:
Autosomal Dominant (AD)

*   Males and females affected equally.
*   No skipping of generations.
*   Father-to-son transmission is possible.
*   Example: Huntington’s Disease.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child is diagnosed with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. Both parents are clinically normal, but are first cousins. Identify the most likely inheritance pattern based on this presentation.
back:
Autosomal Recessive (AR)

*   Horizontal transmission (siblings affected).
*   Associated with consanguinity.
*   Trait often skips generations.
*   Occurs only in homozygotes.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the biological mechanism that prevents affected fathers from passing mitochondrial traits to their children.
back:
Maternal Inheritance

*   Mitochondria are derived strictly from the oocyte.
*   Sperm mitochondria are located in the tail, which does not enter the egg or is degraded after fertilization.
*   Only mothers pass mtDNA to offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the expected phenotypes of daughters born to a father with an X-linked recessive disorder versus a father with an X-linked dominant disorder.
back:
Daughter Phenotypes

*   X-linked Recessive: All daughters are obligate carriers (clinically normal).
*   X-linked Dominant: All daughters are affected.
*   In both cases, sons are unaffected (receive Y from father).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the pedigree characteristics of an X-linked recessive trait regarding sex distribution and generational patterns.
back:
X-linked Recessive (XLR)

*   Males affected significantly more than females.
*   "Criss-cross" inheritance (grandfather to grandson via carrier daughter).
*   Never transmitted male-to-male.
*   Example: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The definitive clinical feature that distinguishes autosomal dominant inheritance from X-linked dominant inheritance in a pedigree is the presence of [___] transmission.
back:
Male-to-male

*   In AD: Possible (father passes autosome).
*   In XLD: Impossible (father only passes Y to sons).
*   All daughters of an XLD father must be affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A female patient with Vitamin D-resistant rickets (X-linked dominant) has a child with an unaffected male. What is the risk that her son will inherit the condition?
back:
50% Risk

*   As a heterozygote (Xx), she has a 50% chance of passing the affected X to any child.
*   X-linked dominant affects both sexes.
*   Risk is equal for sons and daughters of an affected mother.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: How does Lyonization (X-inactivation) affect the clinical expression of X-linked dominant traits in females compared to males?
back:
Variable Expressivity

*   Females: Usually show milder, more variable symptoms due to random X-inactivation.
*   Males: Usually more severe or lethal as they are hemizygous.
*   Example: Rett Syndrome (lethal in males).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between the "Vertical" and "Horizontal" patterns of inheritance seen in family pedigrees.
back:
Pedigree Patterns

*   Vertical: Seen in Autosomal Dominant; every generation has affected individuals.
*   Horizontal: Seen in Autosomal Recessive; affected individuals are usually in a single sibship (same generation).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern where 100% of the children of an affected female are at risk, but 0% of the children of an affected male exhibit the trait.
back:
Mitochondrial Inheritance

*   Exhibits maternal transmission.
*   Affected males never transmit to offspring.
*   High variability due to heteroplasmy.
*   Example: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree showing [___] inheritance, the trait typically appears in every generation, reflecting a vertical pattern of transmission.
back:
Autosomal Dominant.
- Affected individuals usually have an affected parent.
- Males and females are affected with equal frequency.
- Examples: Huntington's disease, Marfan syndrome.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child of healthy consanguineous parents presents with severe photosensitivity and skin tumors. Multiple siblings are affected but the trait is absent in the parents. Identify the likely inheritance pattern.
back:
Autosomal Recessive.
- Characterized by horizontal transmission (siblings affected).
- Trait often skips generations.
- Frequently associated with consanguinity.
- Example: Xeroderma Pigmentosum.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why an affected father cannot pass an X-linked recessive disorder, such as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, to his biological sons.
back:
- Fathers contribute the Y chromosome to sons.
- The mutant X chromosome is only passed to daughters.
- All daughters of an affected father become obligate carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the transmission pattern of an affected father in X-linked dominant inheritance versus autosomal dominant inheritance.
back:
- X-linked Dominant: Father passes to ALL daughters and NO sons.
- Autosomal Dominant: Father has 50% chance to pass to both sons and daughters.
- Distinguishing factor is the sex-biased distribution from the father.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the unique inheritance pattern observed in mitochondrial disorders such as Mitochondrial Diabetes.
back:
Matrilineal (Maternal) Inheritance.
- Only females transmit to offspring.
- All children of an affected mother are affected.
- Affected males never transmit the trait to their children.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In X-linked recessive inheritance, a carrier female (heterozygote) has a [___]% chance of her sons being affected by the disorder.
back:
50%.
- Half of her sons receive the mutant X chromosome.
- Half of her daughters become carriers.
- Typical of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and Hemophilia.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 40-year-old male develops chorea and dementia. His father died of similar symptoms, and a pedigree shows the trait in every generation without bias to gender. Name the mode of inheritance.
back:
Autosomal Dominant.
- Vertical transmission (no skipping).
- Equal male/female distribution.
- High-yield example: Huntington’s Disease (CAG repeat expansion).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain how the biological concept of 'heteroplasmy' accounts for the variable clinical severity seen among siblings in a mitochondrial pedigree.
back:
- Coexistence of mutant and wild-type mtDNA in a cell.
- Random distribution of mitochondria during division.
- Severity depends on the specific ratio of mutant to normal mitochondria inherited.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between X-linked recessive and X-linked dominant patterns regarding the clinical phenotype of heterozygous females.
back:
- X-linked Recessive: Heterozygotes are typically asymptomatic carriers.
- X-linked Dominant: Heterozygotes manifest the disease phenotype.
- Example (Dominant): Vitamin D-resistant Rickets.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Why does an autosomal recessive trait often appear to 'skip' generations in a clinical family history?
back:
- Requires homozygosity (two mutant alleles).
- Trait only appears when two carriers (heterozygotes) reproduce.
- Recessive alleles persist silently in carriers without manifesting the phenotype.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The inheritance pattern where the disease appears in every generation and each affected child has at least one affected parent is [___].
back:
- Autosomal Dominant.
- Also known as vertical transmission.
- Both sexes are affected with equal frequency.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 5-year-old boy presents with difficulty rising from the floor (Gowers' sign); his mother's brother died of a similar muscular condition. Identify the most likely inheritance pattern.
back:
- X-linked Recessive.
- Transmitted through asymptomatic carrier females.
- Primarily affects males due to their single X chromosome.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the biological basis for the strictly maternal inheritance of mitochondrial DNA mutations.
back:
- Mitochondria in the zygote are derived exclusively from the oocyte.
- Paternal mitochondria in the sperm tail are degraded or excluded upon fertilization.
- All children of an affected mother inherit the trait.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A man with Vitamin D-resistant rickets (X-linked dominant) marries an unaffected woman. Contrast the expected clinical status of his sons versus his daughters.
back:
- Sons: 100% normal (receive the father's Y chromosome).
- Daughters: 100% affected (receive the father's mutant X).
- Distinctive lack of male-to-male transmission.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern typically associated with 'horizontal' transmission, where symptoms often skip generations and appear in multiple siblings of normal parents.
back:
- Autosomal Recessive.
- Parents are usually asymptomatic heterozygotes.
- Risk increases significantly with consanguinity.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In mitochondrial disorders, the coexistence of both mutant and wild-type mitochondrial DNA within a single cell is termed [___].
back:
- Heteroplasmy.
- Accounts for variable severity among siblings.
- Determines the 'threshold' for clinical symptom manifestation.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child is diagnosed with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. Pedigree analysis reveals the parents are first cousins. Explain why this family history increases the risk for this specific condition.
back:
- Consanguinity increases the probability of both parents carrying the same rare recessive allele.
- Higher likelihood of homozygous recessive offspring.
- Typical of autosomal recessive metabolic/repair disorders.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why mitochondrial diseases often exhibit a 'threshold effect' regarding the severity of clinical symptoms in different tissues.
back:
- Phenotype depends on the ratio of mutant to wild-type mtDNA (heteroplasmy).
- Tissues with high energy demands (brain, muscle) have lower thresholds for dysfunction.
- Symptoms emerge only when mutant DNA exceeds a critical level.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between Autosomal Dominant and Mitochondrial inheritance patterns regarding the offspring of an affected father.
back:
- Autosomal Dominant: 50% chance of transmission to both sons and daughters.
- Mitochondrial: 0% chance of transmission (paternal mitochondria do not enter the zygote).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Name the specific inheritance pattern where affected females pass the trait to 50% of their sons and 50% of their daughters, as seen in certain forms of Rickets.
back:
- X-linked Dominant.
- Resembles autosomal dominant in females.
- Differentiated by the affected father's transmission (all daughters, no sons).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree where 100% of the offspring of an affected female exhibit the trait, but no offspring of an affected male are ever affected, the pattern of inheritance is [___].
back:
Mitochondrial (Matrilineal) Inheritance.
• Oocytes provide all mitochondria to the zygote.
• Affected males cannot pass the trait to any child (dead-end).
• Both sexes can be affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A rare metabolic disorder appears in multiple siblings of a Pakistani family with a history of consanguinity, while the parents are clinically normal. Identify the likely inheritance pattern.
back:
Autosomal Recessive (AR).
• Common in consanguineous (first-cousin) marriages.
• Horizontal pedigree pattern (siblings affected).
• 25% recurrence risk per pregnancy.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the characteristic transmission direction observed in an Autosomal Dominant (AD) pedigree across multiple generations.
back:
Vertical Transmission.
• Trait appears in every generation (no skipping).
• Every affected child has an affected parent.
• Affects both sexes equally with 50% transmission risk.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the inheritance of X-linked Dominant (XD) and X-linked Recessive (XR) traits when the father is affected and the mother is homozygous normal.
back:
• XD: 100% of daughters affected; 0% of sons affected.
• XR: 100% of daughters are carriers; 0% of sons affected.
• Crucial Rule: Fathers never pass X-linked traits to sons.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Define 'Pleiotropy' within the context of Autosomal Dominant disorders such as Marfan Syndrome.
back: A single gene mutation causing multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects in different organ systems (e.g., skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular symptoms).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The presence of a mixture of both mutant and wild-type mitochondrial DNA within a single cell, leading to variable clinical severity among siblings, is termed [___].
back:
Heteroplasmy.
• Severity depends on the ratio of mutant to normal mitochondria.
• Explains phenotypic variation in mitochondrial diseases.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A young girl is diagnosed with Vitamin D-resistant rickets. Her father is also affected, but her brothers are completely healthy. Specify the inheritance pattern.
back:
X-linked Dominant (XD).
• Affected fathers pass the allele to all daughters.
• Sons are spared as they receive the Y-chromosome from the father.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe how 'Skewed X-inactivation' (Lyonization) allows a female carrier of an X-linked recessive trait to manifest clinical symptoms.
back:
• Random inactivation of the normal X-chromosome in most cells.
• Mutant X remains active, producing the disease phenotype.
• Known as 'manifesting heterozygotes'.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the types of proteins typically involved in Autosomal Dominant vs. Autosomal Recessive disorders.
back:
• AD: Usually structural proteins (e.g., collagen) or receptors.
• AR: Usually enzymatic or catalytic proteins.
• AR typically requires >50% loss of activity for symptoms.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the genetic occurrence where an individual presents with an Autosomal Dominant disorder despite both parents being genotypically normal.
back:
De Novo (New) Mutation.
• Occurs in the parental germ cell.
• No prior family history.
• The individual can now transmit the trait to offspring (50% risk).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The [___] inheritance pattern is characterized by the transmission of a trait from an affected mother to all of her offspring, whereas an affected father never transmits the trait.
back:
• Mitochondrial Inheritance
• Mutations occur in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)
• Only the oocyte (not sperm) contributes mitochondria to the zygote
• Example: Mitochondrial Diabetes

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 40-year-old male presents with progressive chorea and dementia; his father and grandmother died from the same condition. This generational pattern identifies [___] inheritance.
back:
• Autosomal Dominant (AD)
• Shows vertical transmission (no skipped generations)
• Males and females are affected equally
• Example: Huntington’s Disease

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the biological reason why X-linked recessive disorders, such as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, predominantly affect males.
back:
• Males are hemizygous (XY)
• They possess only one X chromosome
• A single recessive mutant allele on the X is expressed immediately
• Females require two mutant alleles to show phenotype

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the expected offspring of an affected father in X-linked dominant inheritance versus autosomal dominant inheritance.
back:
• X-linked Dominant: All daughters are affected; no sons are affected
• Autosomal Dominant: 50% chance for both sons and daughters to be affected
• Result of father providing Y to sons

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the recurrence risk for the next child of a couple who already have one child with Cystic Fibrosis (Autosomal Recessive).
back:
• 25% (1 in 4) chance of being affected
• 50% (2 in 4) chance of being a carrier
• 75% chance of being phenotypically normal
• Independent of the child's sex

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a clinical pedigree, the appearance of a trait in siblings of a single generation but not in their parents is termed [___] transmission.
back:
• Horizontal Transmission
• Characteristic of Autosomal Recessive traits
• Often associated with consanguineous (first-cousin) marriages
• Example: Xeroderma Pigmentosum

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A female carrier of Hemophilia A (X-linked recessive) exhibits mild bleeding tendencies. This phenomenon is explained by the mechanism of [___].
back:
• Lyonization (X-inactivation)
• Random inactivation of one X chromosome in every cell
• Skewed inactivation leads to more cells expressing the mutant allele
• Results in variable expressivity in females

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Discuss the clinical outcome for sons of a mother affected by an X-linked dominant disorder.
back:
• 50% of sons will be affected
• Affected sons inherit the mutated X from the mother
• Symptoms are often more severe in males than females
• Example: Vitamin D-resistant Rickets

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between the effects of a father’s genotype on his sons in X-linked recessive versus Y-linked (holandric) inheritance.
back:
• X-linked Recessive: Father cannot pass the trait to sons
• Y-linked: Father passes the trait to all sons
• Y-chromosome contains the SRY gene
• Holandric traits never affect females

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: How does the inheritance of Autosomal Recessive traits differ between consanguineous and non-consanguineous populations?
back:
• Consanguinity increases the probability that both parents carry the same rare recessive allele
• Leads to higher frequency of homozygous recessive offspring
• Traits appear more frequently in isolated populations
• Skips generations typically

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In pedigree analysis, the appearance of an autosomal recessive trait in a child of unaffected parents is often associated with [___] between the parents.
back:
Consanguinity (mating between close relatives).
- It increases the likelihood that both parents are carriers.
- The recurrence risk for each child is 25%.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 35-year-old female with a mitochondrial myopathy has three children. Describe the risk of transmission to her offspring according to the mitochondrial inheritance pattern.
back:
100% of children will inherit the trait.
- Transmission occurs exclusively through the maternal oocyte cytoplasm.
- Both sons and daughters are equally affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why an affected father with an X-linked recessive disorder, such as Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, cannot pass the trait to his sons.
back:
Fathers contribute only the Y-chromosome to sons.
- All sons inherit the maternal X-chromosome.
- All daughters will be obligate carriers of the paternal mutant X.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the inheritance outcomes for daughters of an affected father in X-linked dominant versus autosomal dominant patterns.
back:
In XD, 100% of daughters are affected.
- In AD, there is only a 50% chance of transmission.
- XD fathers cannot have affected sons if the mother is normal.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the characteristic 'vertical' pedigree pattern where a trait appears in every generation without skipping.
back:
Autosomal Dominant inheritance.
- Each affected individual usually has an affected parent.
- Males and females are affected with equal frequency.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: For a female to express the phenotype of an X-linked recessive disorder, her genotype must typically be [___].
back:
Homozygous recessive.
- She must inherit one mutant X from a carrier/affected mother.
- She must inherit the second mutant X from an affected father.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child presents with Achondroplasia (autosomal dominant), but both parents have a normal phenotype. Suggest the most likely genetic mechanism for this occurrence.
back:
De novo (spontaneous) mutation.
- The mutation occurs in the parental germline.
- Subsequent generations will follow standard autosomal dominant transmission.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the mechanism of 'skewed Lyonization' and its impact on female carriers of X-linked recessive traits.
back:
Random X-inactivation is non-uniform.
- If the normal X is inactivated in most cells, the carrier expresses the trait.
- This leads to 'manifesting heterozygotes' showing mild clinical symptoms.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Differentiate the recurrence risk for siblings of a proband with an autosomal recessive disorder versus the risk for children of a parent with an autosomal dominant disorder.
back:
AR siblings: 25% risk (if both parents are carriers).
- AD offspring: 50% risk (if one parent is affected).
- AR often shows a 'horizontal' pattern in one generation.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Determine the transmission risk for the offspring of a male who is affected by a mitochondrial DNA mutation.
back:
Zero percent transmission risk.
- Mitochondria are not contributed by the sperm to the zygote.
- Mitochondrial diseases stop at the affected male in a pedigree.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In an autosomal dominant pedigree, the characteristic phenomenon where a trait appears in every generation without skipping is termed [___] inheritance.
back:
Vertical inheritance.
- Affected individuals typically have an affected parent.
- Male and female offspring are equally likely to be affected.
- Recurrence risk for offspring of an affected individual is 50%.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child is diagnosed with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. The parents are healthy first cousins, but two of the patient's siblings are also affected. This presentation most likely indicates [___].
back:
Autosomal Recessive inheritance.
- Often associated with consanguinity (cousin marriages).
- Characterized by a horizontal pattern (affected siblings only).
- Parents are asymptomatic obligate carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the biological basis for the lack of paternal transmission in mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS.
back:
Maternal Inheritance.
- Mitochondria in the zygote are derived exclusively from the oocyte.
- Sperm mitochondria are degraded post-fertilization.
- All children of an affected mother are at risk; affected fathers pass to none.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the inheritance of X-linked dominant traits with autosomal dominant traits specifically regarding the daughters of an affected male.
back:
Transmission differences:
- X-linked Dominant: 100% of daughters are affected (father must pass his affected X).
- Autosomal Dominant: 50% of daughters are affected (standard Mendelian segregation).
- Male-to-male transmission is impossible in X-linked dominant.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern characterized by a 'diagonal' transmission where the trait is passed from an affected male through his carrier daughters to his grandsons.
back:
X-linked Recessive inheritance.
- Primarily affects males (hemizygous status).
- Daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.
- Skips generations via healthy female carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A pedigree shows that an affected female transmits a metabolic trait to all of her children regardless of sex, while her affected brother transmits it to none. This pattern is [___].
back:
Mitochondrial inheritance.
- Non-Mendelian cytoplasmic transmission.
- Clinical severity varies due to heteroplasmy (mixture of mutant/wild-type mtDNA).
- Example: Mitochondrial Diabetes.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 45-year-old male presents with Huntington's disease. His mother was affected, but his father was normal. Analyze the recurrence risk for his future children.
back:
50% risk for all children.
- Huntington's follows Autosomal Dominant inheritance.
- Does not skip generations.
- Offspring risk is independent of the child's sex.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe why a female heterozygous for an X-linked recessive mutation, like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, usually remains asymptomatic.
back:
Carrier status and Lyonization.
- Females have two X chromosomes; the normal allele usually compensates.
- X-inactivation (Lyonization) results in a mosaic of cells.
- Usually requires two mutant alleles for female expression.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between the recurrence risks for a couple who already have one child with Cystic Fibrosis (Autosomal Recessive) versus a father who has Achondroplasia (Autosomal Dominant).
back:
Recurrence risk contrast:
- Cystic Fibrosis (AR): 25% risk for each subsequent pregnancy.
- Achondroplasia (AD): 50% risk for each subsequent pregnancy.
- Both sexes are equally likely to inherit either condition.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Regarding Vitamin D-resistant Rickets (X-linked dominant), specify the expected phenotype of sons born to an affected male and a normal female.
back:
100% normal sons.
- Father provides a Y chromosome to all sons.
- Affected X is only passed to daughters.
- Male-to-male transmission never occurs in X-linked inheritance.

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: According to the Mendelian Law of [___], the two alleles for a heritable character separate during gamete formation and end up in different gametes.
back: • Law of Segregation • Ensures each gamete is haploid • Guarantees each gamete receives exactly one allele from an allelic pair

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
coreConcept: Application of Segregation in Recessive Inheritance
front: A couple, both carriers for Albinism (an autosomal recessive condition), has a child with the disorder. Identify the Mendelian principle that explains the inheritance of recessive alleles from phenotypically normal parents.
back: • Law of Segregation • Alleles separate into distinct gametes during meiosis • Unaffected carrier parents can both contribute a recessive allele to form an affected homozygous offspring

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the role of homologous chromosome separation during Meiosis I as the physical basis for the Law of Segregation.
back: • Occurs primarily during Anaphase I • Homologous pairs are pulled to opposite poles • Results in the distribution of different alleles into separate daughter cells

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A neonate is born with a combination of traits that suggests the independent inheritance of two autosomal genes. Contrast how the Law of Segregation differs from Independent Assortment in explaining this multi-gene outcome.
back: • Segregation: Deals with alleles at one locus separating into gametes • Independent Assortment: Deals with multiple loci segregating without influencing each other • Assortment requires separate chromosomes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
coreConcept: Linkage as an Exception to Mendel's Second Law
front: Identify the genetic phenomenon where alleles at different loci are inherited together, representing a direct violation of the Law of Independent Assortment.
back: • Genetic Linkage • Occurs when genes are physically close on the same chromosome • Reduces the frequency of recombination between those specific traits

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: The Mendelian Law of [___] states that the alleles for one trait are distributed into gametes without being influenced by the distribution of alleles for another trait.
back: • Independent Assortment • Applies to genes located on different chromosomes • Facilitates genetic recombination and offspring diversity

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: A clinician notices that in a pedigree with both Sickle Cell Trait and Polydactyly, the presence of one trait does not correlate with the other. Identify the Mendelian law demonstrated by this pattern.
back: • Law of Independent Assortment • Traits are inherited as independent units • Assumes the loci are located on separate chromosomes or far apart

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Explain the mechanism of Metaphase I chromosomal alignment and how a defect in this process would specifically impair the Law of Independent Assortment compared to Segregation.
back: • Independent assortment depends on random bivalent orientation • Segregation depends on homologous separation • Random orientation creates unique paternal/maternal allele combinations

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Contrast the predicted F2 phenotypic results of a dihybrid cross with those of a monohybrid cross, highlighting how Mendel’s two laws operate simultaneously.
back: • Monohybrid (3:1): Demonstrates alleles separating (Segregation) • Dihybrid (9:3:3:1): Demonstrates two traits sorting independently (Assortment) • Assortment generates four distinct phenotypic classes

category: Describe Mendelian Law of Segregation and Law of Independent Assortment
front: Identify the Mendelian principle that ensures a gamete carries only one member of an allelic pair, often referred to as 'gametic purity'.
back: • Law of Segregation • Prevents a single gamete from carrying multiple alleles for the same locus • Ensures the restoration of diploidy after fertilization

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In an autosomal dominant pedigree, an affected individual typically has at least one affected parent, a pattern referred to as [___] inheritance.
back:
Vertical inheritance.
- Affects every generation (no skipping).
- 50% risk for offspring of an affected parent.
- Affects both males and females equally.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A couple in a consanguineous marriage has a child with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. Although the parents are healthy, the risk of their next child being affected is [___].
back:
25% (Autosomal Recessive).
- Parents are obligate carriers (heterozygotes).
- Horizontal transmission (siblings affected).
- Increased frequency in consanguinity.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why X-linked recessive disorders, like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, are almost exclusively expressed in males.
back:
- Males are hemizygous; a single mutant X chromosome causes disease.
- Females have a second normal X allele that masks the mutation.
- Females only express if homozygous or skewed lyonization occurs.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
coreConcept: Paternal Transmission in X-linked Dominant vs. Autosomal Dominant
front: Distinguish the inheritance pattern of an affected father in X-linked dominant traits versus autosomal dominant traits regarding his offspring.
back:
- X-linked Dominant: 100% of daughters are affected; 0% of sons are affected.
- Autosomal Dominant: 50% chance for any child to be affected, regardless of sex.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern where an affected female transmits the trait to all her children, but an affected male never transmits it.
back:
Mitochondrial (Maternal) Inheritance.
- Mitochondria are inherited solely via the oocyte.
- All offspring of an affected mother inherit the mutation.
- Zero paternal transmission (sperm mitochondria are destroyed).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A hallmark of X-linked recessive inheritance in a large multi-generational pedigree is the absolute absence of [___] transmission.
back:
Male-to-male (Father-to-son).
- Fathers contribute only the Y chromosome to their sons.
- All daughters of an affected father will be obligate carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 45-year-old male is diagnosed with Huntington’s Disease. If he is heterozygous, describe the genetic risk to his future children.
back:
- 50% probability for each child to inherit the Huntington allele.
- Follows Autosomal Dominant pattern.
- Equal risk for sons and daughters.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the role of 'Heteroplasmy' in determining the clinical severity of mitochondrial disorders like Mitochondrial Diabetes.
back:
- Cell contains a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA.
- Severity depends on the proportion of mutant DNA.
- Symptoms appear once a 'threshold' of mutant DNA is exceeded.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the sex distribution of affected individuals in Autosomal Recessive versus X-linked Recessive pedigrees.
back:
- Autosomal Recessive: Equal frequency in males and females.
- X-linked Recessive: Predominantly affects males; females are usually asymptomatic carriers or 'skipped'.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the risk to the offspring of a female who is heterozygous for Vitamin D-resistant Rickets (X-linked dominant).
back:
- 50% of sons will be affected.
- 50% of daughters will be affected.
- Mimics autosomal dominant pattern when the mother is the affected parent.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A pedigree showing a [___] inheritance pattern typically reveals affected individuals in every generation and exhibits male-to-male transmission.
back: Autosomal Dominant (AD).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A toddler presents with progressive muscle weakness and Gower’s sign. His mother’s brother died of the same condition, but his father is healthy. Identify the most likely inheritance pattern.
back: X-linked Recessive (XR).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the role of the oocyte in the specific transmission of mitochondrial disorders like Leber’s Hereditary Optic Neuropathy.
back: * Mitochondria are inherited exclusively via the maternal cytoplasm of the oocyte. * Paternal mitochondria located in the sperm tail do not enter or survive in the zygote during fertilization.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish the transmission of an X-linked dominant trait between an affected father and an affected mother regarding their offspring.
back: * Affected Father: Transmits the trait to all of his daughters but none of his sons. * Affected Mother: Transmits the trait to half of her daughters and half of her sons.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: State the significance of consanguinity in the appearance of autosomal recessive disorders within a family.
back: * Increases the probability of both parents carrying the same rare recessive allele. * Results in a "horizontal" pedigree pattern where multiple siblings are affected but parents are normal.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, females are often twice as frequently affected as males, although their symptoms may be milder due to X-inactivation (Lyonization).
back: X-linked Dominant.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A pedigree analysis shows that an affected woman has passed a trait to all of her eight children, both male and female, while an affected male has no affected children. Name the inheritance mode.
