back: Mitochondrial inheritance.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the phenomenon of 'heteroplasmy' and its relationship to the severity of mitochondrial disease.
back: * The coexistence of mutated and normal mtDNA within a single cell. * Disease severity depends on the proportion of mutant mitochondria reaching a critical threshold in high-energy tissues.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the expected phenotypic appearance of a trait in "skipping generations" between autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive patterns.
back: * Autosomal Dominant: Trait rarely skips generations (except in cases of incomplete penetrance). * Autosomal Recessive: Frequently skips generations, appearing only in homozygous offspring of two carrier parents.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Define the term 'Carrier' specifically within the context of autosomal recessive inheritance.
back: * A phenotypically normal individual. * Possesses one normal (dominant) allele and one mutant (recessive) allele at a specific genetic locus.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, all children of an affected mother inherit the trait, but an affected father cannot pass the condition to any of his offspring.
back:
Mitochondrial inheritance.
- Maternally derived via the ovum.
- All offspring of affected females are at risk.
- Affected males never transmit the trait to children.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 5-year-old child presents with severe sun sensitivity and skin cancers. Both parents are healthy but are first cousins. This presentation is characteristic of [___] inheritance.
back:
Autosomal Recessive inheritance.
- Often involves enzyme deficiencies.
- Frequently associated with consanguinity.
- 25% recurrence risk among siblings of the proband.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why males are predominantly affected in X-linked recessive disorders while females typically remain asymptomatic carriers.
back:
Males are hemizygous (XY).
- A single mutant X allele causes the full phenotype.
- Females (XX) have a second normal allele to compensate.
- Expressed in females only if homozygous.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the appearance of 'vertical' versus 'horizontal' transmission in a multi-generational family pedigree.
back:
Vertical (Autosomal Dominant):
- Affected members in every generation.
Horizontal (Autosomal Recessive):
- Affected members usually limited to a single sibship within one generation.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the specific inheritance pattern where an affected male transmits the trait to all of his daughters but none of his sons.
back:
X-linked Dominant inheritance.
- Daughters must receive the father's only X.
- Sons only receive the father's Y.
- Females are often twice as frequently affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A trait that appears in every generation without skipping, where each affected person has at least one affected parent, follows an [___] pattern.
back:
Autosomal Dominant inheritance.
- Equal frequency in both sexes.
- No skipped generations (full penetrance assumed).
- 50% transmission risk from an affected heterozygote.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A boy is diagnosed with Hemophilia A. His maternal grandfather was also affected, but his parents are healthy. This clinical history suggests [___] inheritance.
back:
X-linked Recessive inheritance.
- Trait 'skips' generations via carrier females.
- Maternal grandfather to grandson transmission is common.
- Obligate carrier status for the mother.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe how the biological mechanism of 'heteroplasmy' leads to variable clinical severity in mitochondrial diseases.
back:
Mixed population of mtDNA.
- Cells contain varying ratios of mutant/wild-type mitochondria.
- Random distribution during mitosis leads to differing tissue loads.
- Threshold effect determines clinical manifestation.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between X-linked recessive and X-linked dominant patterns regarding the phenotype of heterozygous females.
back:
X-linked Recessive:
- Heterozygotes are phenotypically normal carriers.
X-linked Dominant:
- Heterozygotes express the clinical disease (e.g., Vitamin D resistant rickets).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: State the mathematical risk of an offspring inheriting an Autosomal Dominant disorder when one parent is a heterozygote and the other is homozygous normal.
back:
50% risk per pregnancy.
- Calculated as 1 in 2 chance.
- Risk is independent of the child's sex.
- Typical of Huntington’s disease inheritance.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In mitochondrial inheritance, because the zygote's mitochondria are derived exclusively from the oocyte, the trait is transmitted to offspring only by [___].
back:
• Maternal inheritance
• Affected females pass the trait to all offspring
• Affected males pass the trait to none of their children

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 4-year-old boy presents with pseudohypertrophy of the calves and difficulty rising from a seated position (Gower's sign). His sisters and parents are asymptomatic. Identify the most likely inheritance pattern.
back:
• X-linked recessive
• Primarily affects males (hemizygous)
• Transmitted via asymptomatic carrier females

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why autosomal dominant disorders, such as Huntington’s disease, typically show a 'vertical' pattern of transmission in a pedigree.
back:
• Phenotype expressed in heterozygotes (one mutant allele required)
• Trait appears in every generation without skipping
• Each affected individual usually has an affected parent

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the predicted offspring of an affected father in X-linked dominant inheritance (e.g., Vitamin D-resistant Rickets) with those in autosomal dominant inheritance.
back:
• X-linked Dominant: 100% of daughters affected; 0% of sons affected
• Autosomal Dominant: 50% chance of inheritance for both sons and daughters

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern most strongly associated with 'horizontal' distribution among siblings and an increased prevalence in consanguineous families.
back:
• Autosomal Recessive
• Often skips generations (parents are unaffected carriers)
• Requires two mutant alleles (homozygosity) for expression

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The definitive exclusion of [___] transmission is a hallmark finding in a pedigree that rules out autosomal dominant inheritance in favor of X-linked recessive inheritance.
back:
• Male-to-male (father-to-son)
• Fathers provide only the Y chromosome to sons
• Sons must inherit the mutant X from the mother

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A woman with MERRF syndrome has three children; all exhibit varying severities of myopathy. Her brother is also affected but has two completely healthy children. Explain the underlying genetic principle.
back:
• Mitochondrial inheritance
• Only females transmit the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations
• Males do not pass mitochondria to zygotes

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the mechanism of 'heteroplasmy' and its effect on phenotypic severity in mitochondrial disorders.
back:
• Coexistence of mutant and wild-type mtDNA in one cell
• Severity depends on the ratio of mutant to normal mitochondria
• Random segregation causes variable expressivity among siblings

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the clinical phenotype of a heterozygous female in X-linked recessive versus X-linked dominant inheritance.
back:
• X-linked Recessive: Female is an asymptomatic carrier
• X-linked Dominant: Female is clinically affected
• Dominant traits require only one active mutant X

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Determine the carrier probability for a healthy sibling of a child diagnosed with Xeroderma Pigmentosum (Autosomal Recessive).
back:
• 2/3 (67%)
• Parents are obligate carriers (Aa x Aa)
• Healthy sibling cannot be 'aa', leaving only AA, Aa, or aA genotypes

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree showing a [___] inheritance pattern, the disease typically appears in siblings but not in their parents (horizontal transmission), often associated with consanguineous marriages.
back:
* Autosomal Recessive (AR)
* Requires homozygous mutant alleles for phenotypic expression
* Each sibling has a 25% chance of being affected if parents are carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A woman with a mitochondrial disorder has four children (two males, two females). All of them exhibit the disease. Both sons marry healthy women and have only healthy children. Name the inheritance pattern.
back:
* Mitochondrial (Matrilineal) Inheritance
* Traits are passed only by females to all offspring
* Males cannot transmit the trait because sperm contribute negligible mitochondria.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why Autosomal Dominant (AD) traits are described as exhibiting 'Vertical Transmission' in a medical pedigree.
back:
* The trait appears in every generation without skipping
* Every affected individual must have at least one affected parent
* Affected individuals have a 50% chance of passing the trait to any offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the expected inheritance of an X-linked Dominant (XLD) trait versus an Autosomal Dominant (AD) trait from an affected father to his sons.
back:
* XLD: 0% of sons are affected (they inherit the Y chromosome)
* AD: 50% of sons are affected (they inherit an autosome)
* XLD fathers pass the trait to 100% of their daughters.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: State the biological reason why male-to-male transmission is never observed in X-linked Recessive (XLR) disorders.
back:
* Fathers always contribute their Y chromosome to their sons
* The X-linked mutant allele is only passed from father to daughters
* Affected males must inherit the mutant X from their mother.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In Vitamin D-resistant rickets, which follows an [___] pattern, an affected male will always have 100% affected daughters and 0% affected sons.
back:
* X-linked Dominant (XLD)
* Only one copy of the dominant allele is needed on the X chromosome
* Females are typically more frequently (but less severely) affected than males.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A couple is concerned because both are carriers for Galactosemia (an Autosomal Recessive trait). If they have an unaffected child, what is the probability that this child is a carrier?
back:
* 2/3 (or 66.7%)
* Among unaffected children of two carriers, the possible genotypes are homozygous normal (1) or carrier (2)
* The affected (homozygous recessive) possibility is excluded.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the concept of 'Criss-cross Inheritance' as it applies to X-linked Recessive traits.
back:
* The trait is transmitted from an affected father to his grandson through a carrier daughter
* Skip-generation pattern is typical
* Males are the primary group affected due to hemizygosity.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between 'Horizontal' and 'Vertical' transmission based on the specific generation types affected in a family tree.
back:
* Horizontal: Affected individuals are in the same generation (typical of AR)
* Vertical: Affected individuals appear in consecutive generations (typical of AD)
* AR skips generations; AD does not.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the primary reason why mitochondrial DNA mutations result in variable clinical severity among siblings from the same affected mother.
back:
* Heteroplasmy
* Cell contains a mix of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA
* Random distribution of mitochondria during oogenesis leads to varying proportions of mutant DNA.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Genetic disorders that manifest in the heterozygous state and often involve mutations in structural proteins or receptors are typically inherited in an [___] pattern.
back:
Autosomal Dominant (AD)
- Manifests with one mutant allele.
- Vertical transmission (no skipped generations).
- Examples: Huntington’s disease, Marfan syndrome.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 40-year-old female with MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged Red Fibers) has four children, all of whom show varying degrees of muscle weakness. Her husband is healthy. Identify the inheritance pattern.
back:
Mitochondrial (Matrilineal) Inheritance
- Transmitted only through the mother.
- All offspring of an affected female are at risk.
- High variability due to heteroplasmy.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why daughters of a male affected by an X-linked recessive disorder (e.g., Hemophilia) are termed "obligate carriers."
back: The father must pass his only X chromosome (carrying the mutation) to all daughters. They receive a normal X from their mother, making them heterozygous carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast X-linked dominant inheritance with autosomal dominant inheritance using the offspring of an affected male as the clinical marker.
back:
- X-linked Dominant: 100% of daughters are affected; 0% of sons are affected.
- Autosomal Dominant: 50% of daughters are affected; 50% of sons are affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern characterized by horizontal transmission (affected siblings) and a higher incidence in consanguineous families.
back:
Autosomal Recessive (AR)
- Requires two mutant alleles (homozygosity).
- Skips generations frequently.
- Examples: Cystic Fibrosis, PKU, Xeroderma Pigmentosum.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: For a female carrier of an X-linked recessive disorder, the probability of any specific son being phenotypically affected is [___]%.
back:
50%
- She has a 50% chance of passing the mutant X to each son.
- 50% of her daughters will be carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Two phenotypically normal parents have a child with Xeroderma Pigmentosum. What is the probability that their next child will be a healthy (non-carrier) child?
back:
25%
- Recurrence risk: 25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% healthy (non-carrier).
- This follows Mendelian Autosomal Recessive ratios.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the physiological reason why mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations are never transmitted from an affected father to his offspring.
back: During fertilization, the sperm's mitochondria are located in the tail, which is shed or degraded; the zygote’s mitochondria are derived entirely from the oocyte cytoplasm.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the risk to offspring when one parent is affected by an Autosomal Dominant trait versus an Autosomal Recessive trait (assuming the other parent is homozygous normal).
back:
- AD: 50% risk of disease for all offspring.
- AR: 0% risk of disease; 100% risk of the offspring becoming carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree for Vitamin D-resistant Rickets (X-linked dominant), state the hallmark finding regarding affected fathers and their daughters.
back: All daughters of an affected father will be affected (100%), as they must inherit his only (mutant) X chromosome.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, the trait is transmitted exclusively by females to all their offspring, as the zygote's cytoplasm and organelles are derived solely from the oocyte.
back:
● Mitochondrial inheritance
● Mothers pass to 100% of children
● Affected males never transmit to offspring
● High phenotypic variability due to heteroplasmy

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 40-year-old male with progressive chorea and dementia has an affected father and two affected siblings. This vertical transmission pattern with a 50% recurrence risk suggests [___] inheritance.
back:
● Autosomal Dominant (AD)
● Observed in every generation (vertical)
● Both sexes affected equally
● Example: Huntington’s Disease

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the specific transmission pattern from an affected male to his offspring in X-linked dominant conditions like Vitamin D-resistant rickets.
back:
● 100% of daughters are affected
● 0% of sons are affected
● No male-to-male transmission
● Daughters inherit the father's single affected X chromosome

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A pedigree shows siblings affected by Xeroderma Pigmentosum, but their parents are healthy. Contrast this 'horizontal' pattern with the 'vertical' pattern of Huntington’s Disease.
back:
● Horizontal: Autosomal Recessive (skips generations)
● Vertical: Autosomal Dominant (present in all generations)
● Consanguinity: Common risk factor for horizontal patterns
● Recurrence risk: 25% for AR, 50% for AD

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Why does consanguinity significantly increase the incidence of disorders like Phenylketonuria (PKU) in specific populations?
back:
● Increases probability of mating between two carriers
● Characteristic of Autosomal Recessive traits
● Results in homozygous offspring from shared ancestors
● Skips generations in pedigrees

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Males are described as [___] for X-linked genes because they possess only one X chromosome, causing recessive alleles to manifest phenotypically even without a second copy.
back:
● Hemizygous
● Explains male predominance in XLR disorders
● Only one mutant allele needed for disease
● Examples: Hemophilia, DMD

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A mother passes a trait to all five children, but her affected brother has no affected offspring. Which inheritance pattern does this scenario definitively identify?
back:
● Mitochondrial inheritance
● Maternal lineage transmission only
● Affected males are genetic dead-ends for the trait
● Example: Mitochondrial Diabetes

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the inheritance risks for the children of a woman who is a carrier for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (X-linked Recessive).
back:
● 50% of sons will be affected
● 50% of daughters will be carriers
● No male-to-male transmission from affected fathers
● Skips generations (grandfather to grandson)

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between X-linked recessive and autosomal recessive patterns regarding the frequency of affected females.
back:
● XLR: Females rarely affected (need two mutant X's or skewed Lyonization)
● AR: Both sexes affected with equal frequency
● XLR: Skips generations via carrier females
● AR: Horizontal distribution among siblings

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the primary characteristic of an Autosomal Dominant trait in a pedigree that excludes X-linked inheritance.
back:
● Presence of male-to-male transmission
● Vertical inheritance (no skipping generations)
● 50% transmission regardless of offspring gender
● Both sexes can transmit to both sexes

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In Autosomal Dominant (AD) inheritance, the trait typically appears in every generation, reflecting a [___] pattern of transmission.
back:
Vertical transmission
• Affected individuals usually have at least one affected parent.
• Male-to-male transmission is possible.
• Each offspring of an affected parent has a 50% risk.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A Pakistani couple, who are first cousins, present with a child suffering from Beta-thalassemia. This presentation and family history are hallmarks of an [___] inheritance pattern.
back:
Autosomal Recessive (AR)
• Frequently associated with consanguinity (cousin marriages).
• Typically skips generations (horizontal pattern).
• Parents are usually asymptomatic heterozygous carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the biological basis for the unique inheritance pattern of mitochondrial disorders like MELAS.
back:
Maternal Inheritance
• Mitochondria are inherited exclusively from the mother's oocyte.
• Affected mothers pass the trait to 100% of children.
• Affected fathers never transmit the trait to offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the phenotypic expression of an X-linked Recessive (XLR) trait between a male and a female carrying one mutant allele.
back:
Hemizygosity vs. Heterozygosity
• Males (Hemizygous): Always express the trait (only one X chromosome).
• Females (Heterozygous): Usually asymptomatic carriers.
• Skewed lyonization (X-inactivation) may cause mild symptoms in females.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the risk to the offspring of a male affected by an X-linked Dominant disorder (e.g., Vitamin D-resistant rickets).
back:
Paternal XLD Transmission
• 100% of daughters will be affected (receive X from father).
• 0% of sons will be affected (receive Y from father).
• No male-to-male transmission occurs.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy, an affected male's daughters are referred to as [___] regarding their genetic status.
back:
Obligate Carriers
• They must inherit the single mutant X from their father.
• They have a 50% risk of passing the mutant X to their sons.
• Their sons then have a 50% chance of disease.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 40-year-old male presents with chorea and personality changes. His father died of similar symptoms. If this is Huntington's Disease, identify the risk for his unborn child.
back:
50% Offspring Risk (AD Pattern)
• Huntington's is an Autosomal Dominant trait.
• Displays anticipation (worsening in successive generations).
• Caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansions.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the mechanism of 'Heteroplasmy' and its effect on the severity of mitochondrial diseases.
back:
Mitochondrial Heteroplasmy
• Mixture of normal (wild-type) and mutant mtDNA within one cell.
• Severity depends on the proportion of mutant mitochondria.
• Leads to highly variable clinical phenotypes within the same family.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between 'Horizontal' and 'Vertical' transmission observed in pedigree analysis.
back:
Pedigree Transmission Patterns
• Vertical: Seen in AD; trait found in every generation.
• Horizontal: Seen in AR; siblings affected while parents/offspring are often normal.
• Vertical involves direct ancestry; Horizontal involves siblings.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern where males and females are affected equally, but the trait can only be transmitted by females.
back:
Mitochondrial Inheritance
• Affects both sexes with equal likelihood.
• Sperm do not contribute mitochondria to the zygote.
• All offspring of an affected female are affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, only one copy of a mutant allele is necessary for the disease phenotype to be expressed, typically showing vertical transmission in every generation.
back:
Autosomal Dominant (AD)
* Single mutant allele causes disease.
* 50% risk for offspring.
* Example: Huntington’s Disease.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 5-year-old child presents with extreme sensitivity to sunlight (Xeroderma Pigmentosum). His parents are healthy first cousins. Identify the most likely inheritance pattern.
back:
Autosomal Recessive (AR)
* Requires two mutant alleles (homozygous).
* Often associated with consanguinity.
* 25% risk for offspring of carrier parents.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why mitochondrial disorders, such as MELAS, are exclusively transmitted by females to all their offspring, while affected males never transmit the trait.
back:
Maternal Inheritance
* Mitochondria are inherited via the oocyte (cytoplasm).
* Spermatozoa do not contribute mitochondria to the zygote.
* All children of an affected mother inherit the mutation.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the inheritance outcomes for daughters of an affected male in X-linked dominant versus X-linked recessive conditions.
back:
X-linked Transmission
* X-linked Dominant: 100% of daughters are affected.
* X-linked Recessive: 100% of daughters are carriers (phenotypically normal).
* Sons are never affected by their father in either.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the genetic status of a male regarding genes on the X-chromosome that explains why recessive traits like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy manifest predominantly in males.
back:
Hemizygosity
* Males have only one X chromosome.
* A single recessive allele on the X chromosome is always expressed.
* No corresponding allele on the Y chromosome to mask it.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The inheritance pattern where both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote state, such as in the AB blood group, is termed [___].
back:
Codominance
* Both alleles are equally dominant.
* Phenotype includes distinct expressions of both alleles.
* Neither allele is masked.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A male child with Vitamin D-resistant rickets has an affected mother and an unaffected father. His sister is also affected. Identify the inheritance mode.
back:
X-linked Dominant
* Affected females pass the trait to 50% of sons and daughters.
* Characterized by an excess of affected females in the pedigree.
* Example: Hypophosphatemic Rickets.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the concept of 'variable expressivity' in the context of an autosomal dominant disorder like Neurofibromatosis Type 1.
back:
Variable Expressivity
* Genotype is constant but phenotype severity varies.
* One individual may have mild 'Café-au-lait' spots, while another has severe neurofibromas.
* Differs from penetrance (all-or-none).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between 'vertical' and 'horizontal' transmission patterns on a pedigree chart.
back:
Pedigree Patterns
* Vertical: Found in Autosomal Dominant (seen in every generation).
* Horizontal: Found in Autosomal Recessive (seen in siblings/one generation; parents normal).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the primary risk factor in Pakistani populations that significantly increases the incidence of autosomal recessive disorders.
back:
Consanguinity
* Marriage between close relatives (first cousins).
* Increases the probability of offspring inheriting identical mutant alleles from a common ancestor.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In mitochondrial inheritance patterns, an affected male cannot pass the trait to any of his offspring, a phenomenon known as [___] inheritance.
back:
* Maternal inheritance.
* Mitochondria are inherited exclusively via the oocyte.
* Sperm mitochondria do not contribute to the zygote's mitochondrial pool.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A couple, both phenotypically normal, has a child with Phenylketonuria. Determine the probability that their next child will be a phenotypically normal carrier of the mutant gene.
back:
* 50% (1/2).
* Parents are obligate heterozygotes (Aa).
* Mendelian ratio for Aa x Aa is 1:2:1 (25% AA, 50% Aa, 25% aa).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why X-linked recessive disorders, such as Hemophilia A, are expressed almost exclusively in males.
back:
* Males are hemizygous (XY).
* A single mutant X chromosome causes disease expression.
* Females (XX) typically require two mutant alleles or skewed X-inactivation.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the transmission patterns of an affected father in Autosomal Dominant versus X-linked Dominant traits.
back:
* Autosomal Dominant: 50% risk for both sons and daughters.
* X-linked Dominant: 100% of daughters affected; 0% of sons affected.
* Father cannot pass X-linked traits to sons.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern characterized by 'vertical transmission,' where the trait appears in every generation without skipping, affecting both sexes equally.
back:
* Autosomal Dominant.
* Only one mutant allele is required for phenotype expression.
* Every affected individual typically has an affected parent.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In X-linked recessive pedigrees, an unaffected mother of an affected son is described as an [___].
back:
* Obligate Carrier.
* She possesses one mutant X chromosome.
* Each son has a 50% risk of being affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A mother with a mitochondrial myopathy has four children; all four exhibit varying degrees of muscle weakness and lactic acidosis. Name the biological phenomenon explaining this variable severity.
back:
* Heteroplasmy.
* Mixture of mutant and wild-type mitochondrial DNA in cells.
* Severity depends on the proportion of mutant mitochondria inherited.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the mechanism by which consanguineous marriages increase the incidence of rare genetic disorders in certain populations.
back:
* Increases probability of mating between two carriers of the same rare allele.
* Leads to homozygous recessive offspring.
* Characteristic of Autosomal Recessive inheritance.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Differentiate between the 'horizontal' and 'vertical' pedigree patterns associated with Mendelian traits.
back:
* Horizontal: Autosomal Recessive (seen in siblings, skips generations).
* Vertical: Autosomal Dominant (seen in every generation, parent-to-child).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern where an affected female has a 50% chance of passing the trait to both sons and daughters, regardless of the father's genotype.
back:
* X-linked Dominant (or Autosomal Dominant).
* For X-linked Dominant, both sexes receive her affected X.
* Mimics autosomal dominant when transmitted by the mother.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The characteristic pattern of [___] inheritance is 'horizontal' transmission, where affected individuals are typically siblings in one generation rather than appearing in every generation.
back: * Autosomal Recessive. * Often involves consanguinity (cousin marriages). * 25% recurrence risk for children of carrier parents.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 5-year-old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and is found to have a maternal uncle who died of a similar condition. Identify the most likely inheritance pattern.
back: * X-linked Recessive. * Mother is an asymptomatic carrier. * 50% risk of inheritance for each son of a carrier mother.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the genetic mechanism that results in all children of an affected mother inheriting a mitochondrial disorder, while no children of an affected father inherit the trait.
back: * Maternal Inheritance. * The zygote receives mitochondria almost exclusively from the oocyte. * Sperm mitochondria are degraded or excluded during fertilization.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between X-linked dominant and Autosomal dominant patterns based exclusively on the offspring of an affected male and an unaffected female.
back: * X-linked Dominant: All daughters are affected, but zero sons are affected. * Autosomal Dominant: There is a 50% chance for both sons and daughters to be affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the primary pedigree observation that establishes a trait is likely Autosomal Dominant rather than a recessive form of inheritance.
back: * Vertical transmission pattern (appears in every generation). * Each affected person has an affected parent. * Males and females are affected in equal proportions.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree showing Vitamin D-resistant rickets, an affected male transmits the trait to [___] of his daughters but none of his sons.
back: * 100%. * Characteristic of X-linked Dominant inheritance. * Father provides his only X chromosome (carrying the mutation) to all female offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A child is diagnosed with Xeroderma Pigmentosum; the parents are healthy but are first cousins. Describe the inheritance pattern and the typical pedigree distribution for this case.
back: * Autosomal Recessive. * 'Horizontal' pattern among siblings. * Increased risk due to consanguinity bringing rare recessive alleles together.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the mechanism of 'Skewed Lyonization' and how it permits a female carrier to manifest a typically X-linked recessive disorder.
back: * Non-random X-inactivation. * Most cells inactivate the X chromosome carrying the normal allele. * The mutant 'recessive' allele on the active X is expressed phenotypically.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the carrier status of males and females in X-linked Recessive versus Autosomal Recessive inheritance cycles.
back: * X-linked: Only females are typically carriers; males are either affected or normal. * Autosomal: Both sexes can be asymptomatic carriers. * AR requires two carrier parents.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the unique biochemical source of the 37 genes that are inherited through the maternal cytoplasm and are associated with Mitochondrial Diabetes.
back: * Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). * Circular genome located in the mitochondrial matrix. * Exclusively maternal transmission to all offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In an Autosomal Dominant pedigree, the probability of an affected heterozygous parent passing the trait to their offspring, regardless of sex, is [___]%.
back:
• 50% recurrence risk
• Vertical transmission (present in every generation)
• Males and females are affected equally
• No skipped generations

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A healthy couple has a child with Cystic Fibrosis (ΔF508 mutation). Identify the most likely inheritance pattern and the recurrence risk for their next pregnancy.
back:
• Autosomal Recessive
• 25% (1 in 4) recurrence risk
• Horizontal transmission (siblings affected, parents healthy)
• Increased risk with consanguinity

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations are exclusively transmitted through the maternal line.
back:
• Oocytes provide nearly all cytoplasm and organelles
• Sperm mitochondria are degraded post-fertilization
• Affected mothers pass to all children
• Affected fathers pass to none

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast Vitamin D-resistant Rickets (X-linked Dominant) with Huntington’s Disease (Autosomal Dominant) regarding the offspring of an affected father.
back:
• X-linked Dominant: 100% daughters affected; 0% sons affected (no male-to-male)
• Autosomal Dominant: 50% risk for all children regardless of sex
• X-linked: Father gives Y to sons and X to daughters

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Why are X-linked recessive disorders like Hemophilia A typically expressed only in males?
back:
• Males are hemizygous (only one X chromosome)
• Single mutant allele causes full phenotype
• Females require two mutant alleles or skewed lyonization
• Characteristic skip-generation pattern via carrier females

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: The likelihood of encountering an Autosomal Recessive trait, such as Thalassemia, increases significantly in populations where [___] (marriage between close relatives) is common.
back:
• Consanguinity
• Increases homozygosity of rare recessive alleles
• Leads to horizontal pedigree patterns
• High prevalence in specific Pakistani demographics

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A mother with MERRF syndrome has three children with varying severities of the disease (severe, mild, and asymptomatic). Identify the genetic phenomenon explaining this variability.
back:
• Heteroplasmy
• Co-existence of mutant and wild-type mtDNA
• Severity depends on the proportion of mutant mitochondria received
• Random distribution during oocyte formation

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe how skewed X-inactivation (Lyonization) manifests in a female carrier of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD).
back:
• One X is randomly inactivated (Barr body)
• Skewed: Functional X is preferentially inactivated
• Result: Manifesting heterozygote (female shows symptoms)
• Usually prevents total silencing of mutant allele

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between X-linked recessive and autosomal recessive patterns regarding male-to-male transmission in a pedigree.
back:
• X-linked Recessive: Zero male-to-male transmission (Father gives Y to sons)
• Autosomal Recessive: Male-to-male transmission is possible
• X-linked: Affected males make all daughters obligate carriers

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a clinical genetic pedigree, identify the term for the first affected family member seeking medical attention and their symbolic representation.
back:
• Proband (or Propositus/Proposita)
• Indicated by an arrow pointing to the individual's symbol
• Serves as the starting point for the genealogical study

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree, [___] inheritance is characterized by "horizontal" transmission, where the trait often appears in siblings but not their parents, particularly in consanguineous families.
back:
Autosomal Recessive (AR) inheritance.
* Both parents are typically asymptomatic carriers.
* 25% recurrence risk for each sibling.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 4-year-old boy presents with calf pseudo-hypertrophy and difficulty climbing stairs. His maternal uncle died of a similar condition. Identify the likely mode of inheritance.
back:
X-linked Recessive (XR) inheritance.
* Common in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD).
* Transmitted by carrier females to 50% of sons.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why mitochondrial DNA disorders are transmitted exclusively from the mother to all her children.
back:
* Maternal inheritance: The zygote's mitochondria are derived entirely from the ovum.
* Sperm mitochondria are located in the tail and are lost/degraded at fertilization.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast X-linked Dominant and Autosomal Dominant inheritance based on the offspring of an affected father and a healthy mother.
back:
* X-linked Dominant: All daughters are affected; no sons are affected.
* Autosomal Dominant: 50% risk for all children regardless of sex.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Identify the inheritance pattern where a single copy of a mutant allele on a non-sex chromosome causes the disease and appears in every generation.
back:
Autosomal Dominant (AD) inheritance.
* Characterized by "vertical" transmission.
* Example: Huntington’s Disease.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A trait that is expressed in a male but requires two copies of the allele to be expressed in a female is termed [___].
back:
X-linked Recessive.
* Males are hemizygous (one X).
* Females require two mutant alleles (homozygous) or skewed inactivation to manifest.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A man with X-linked dominant Vitamin D-resistant rickets marries a healthy woman. Describe the expected phenotypic outcomes for his sons.
back:
* All sons will be healthy.
* A father passes his Y chromosome to sons, never the affected X.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the mechanism of "Skewed X-inactivation" and its effect on a female carrier of Hemophilia A.
back:
* Skewed Lyonization: Random inactivation of the X carrying the normal allele in most cells.
* Leads to symptomatic carrier status (bleeding tendencies) despite being genotypically heterozygous.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between the genetic terms "Penetrance" and "Variable Expressivity."
back:
* Penetrance: The percentage of individuals with a genotype who show any phenotype (all-or-none).
* Expressivity: The severity of the phenotype among those who show it.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Define the term "Proband" (Propositus/Proposita) in the context of clinical genetics.
back:
* The first affected family member who brings the pedigree to the attention of medical professionals.
* Indicated by an arrow in pedigree charts.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In [___] inheritance, a single copy of a mutant allele on a non-sex chromosome is sufficient to produce the disease phenotype in every generation.
back:
Autosomal dominant.
- Vertical transmission (no skipped generations).
- 50% recurrence risk for offspring.
- Males and females affected equally.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 5-year-old boy presents with progressive muscle weakness and pseudohypertrophy of the calves. His mother is asymptomatic, but her brother died of a similar condition. Identify the mode of inheritance.
back:
X-linked recessive.
- Primarily affects males.
- Females act as carriers.
- No male-to-male transmission.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain the role of the oocyte in the transmission of disorders such as MELAS and MERRF.
back:
Mitochondrial inheritance.
- Transmitted exclusively through the maternal line.
- Oocytes contribute mitochondria to the zygote; sperm do not.
- Affected mothers pass traits to all children.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the transmission pattern of an X-linked dominant disorder with an autosomal dominant disorder when the father is the only affected parent.
back:
- X-linked dominant: 100% of daughters are affected; 0% of sons are affected.
- Autosomal dominant: 50% of both daughters and sons are affected.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Discuss the significance of consanguinity in the pedigree of a family presenting with Xeroderma Pigmentosum.
back:
- Characteristic of autosomal recessive traits.
- Increases the likelihood of both parents being carriers of the same rare mutation.
- Results in a 25% risk for offspring.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In autosomal recessive inheritance, an individual who inherits two different mutant alleles at the same locus is termed a [___].
back:
Compound heterozygote.
- Common in conditions like cystic fibrosis or PKU.
- Results in disease phenotype despite different specific mutations.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A female patient is diagnosed with Vitamin D-resistant rickets. Her father is affected, but her mother is not. All her sisters are affected, but none of her brothers. Identify the inheritance pattern.
back:
X-linked dominant.
- Affected males pass trait to all daughters.
- Affected males pass trait to zero sons.
- No skipped generations.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: How does the concept of heteroplasmy explain the phenotypic variation seen in siblings with the same mitochondrial DNA mutation?
back:
- Random distribution of mutant and wild-type mitochondria during cell division.
- Severity depends on the proportion of mutant mitochondria in specific tissues.
- Leads to variable clinical expression.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between the carrier risks for siblings of an affected child in autosomal recessive versus autosomal dominant disorders (assuming unaffected parents).
back:
- Autosomal Recessive: 2/3 (67%) chance of being a carrier.
- Autosomal Dominant: Negligible (usually implies a de novo mutation or incomplete penetrance).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Define the term used for males who possess only one X chromosome and therefore express all genes located on it, regardless of dominance.
back:
Hemizygous.
- Explains why X-linked recessive traits manifest in males.
- Single allele determines the phenotype.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: In a standard genetic pedigree, a square that is completely filled or shaded represents an [___].
back:
• Affected male
• Indicates the individual manifests the phenotypic trait or disease being studied.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A pedigree shows a double horizontal line connecting a male and female who have three children with an autosomal recessive disorder. This specific symbol indicates [___].
back:
• Consanguineous mating
• Represents a union between biologically related individuals (e.g., first cousins).
• High clinical relevance for rare recessive traits.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Explain the significance of an arrow pointing toward a specific symbol in a pedigree.
back:
• Identifies the Proband (Propositus/Proposita)
• The first family member who brings the trait to medical attention.
• Serves as the index case for genealogical study.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Contrast the pedigree representation of an obligate carrier in an X-linked recessive trait versus a standard affected individual.
back:
• Carrier: A circle containing a central dot or a half-shaded symbol.
• Affected: A symbol (square or circle) that is entirely filled/shaded.
• Carriers harbor the genotype without expressing the full phenotype.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Identify the pedigree symbol used to represent a miscarriage or spontaneous abortion of unspecified gender.
back:
• Small triangle (sometimes a small diamond)
• Used to document pregnancy loss in the family history.
• May include a diagonal line to indicate the loss.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: In a pedigree, a horizontal line connecting a square and a circle is called a [___] line.
back:
• Mating or Marriage line
• Represents the parental union.
• A vertical line descending from it (the sibship line) leads to offspring.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A pedigree for a family with Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy shows a circle with a dot in the center. What genetic status does this symbol convey?
back:
• X-linked recessive carrier female
• Indicates she possesses one mutant allele on one X chromosome.
• She is phenotypically normal but can transmit the trait.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Explain how generations and individuals are systematically identified within a pedigree to facilitate clinical discussion.
back:
• Generations: Roman numerals (I, II, III) from oldest to youngest.
• Individuals: Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3) from left to right within each generation.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Distinguish between the symbols for monozygotic twins and dizygotic twins in a pedigree.
back:
• Monozygotic: Two symbols branching from one point with a connecting horizontal line.
• Dizygotic: Two symbols branching from one point without a horizontal connection.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Identify the meaning of a diagonal line drawn through a pedigree symbol.
back:
• Deceased individual
• Indicates the person is no longer living.
• Crucial for documenting mortality patterns in familial diseases.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In a pedigree showing [___] inheritance, the trait typically appears in every generation without skipping, and both males and females are equally likely to be affected.
back: Autosomal Dominant (AD). - Vertical transmission (no skipping). - 50% recurrence risk for offspring. - Male-to-male transmission is possible.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A 4-year-old child presents with intellectual disability and musty odor. The parents are healthy first cousins. This pedigree likely represents [___] inheritance.
back: Autosomal Recessive (AR). - Horizontal pattern (skips generations). - 25% risk to offspring of carrier parents. - Consanguinity (cousin marriage) increases prevalence.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Describe the transmission mechanism of mitochondrial traits, such as MERRF or MELAS, within a family.
back: Matrilineal Inheritance. - Transmitted only by mothers to all offspring. - Affected fathers pass the trait to 0% of children. - Phenotypic severity varies due to heteroplasmy.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Contrast the transmission pattern of an affected father in X-linked dominant inheritance versus autosomal dominant inheritance.
back: X-linked Dominant: Affected fathers pass the trait to all daughters but no sons. - Autosomal Dominant: Affected fathers have a 50% chance of passing to any child.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Explain why males are primarily affected in X-linked recessive disorders like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
back: Hemizygosity. - Males have only one X chromosome. - A single mutant allele is sufficient to express phenotype. - No matching allele on Y chromosome to mask defect.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In X-linked recessive inheritance, a male with one mutant allele is described as [___] because he lacks a second X chromosome to mask the recessive trait.
back: Hemizygous. - Only one allele present at a locus. - Always expresses X-linked recessive phenotypes. - Daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: A healthy woman whose brother has Hemophilia A (X-linked recessive) is a carrier. Identify the risk to her future sons and daughters.
back: Sons: 50% risk of being affected. - Daughters: 50% risk of being carriers. - Offspring inherit the mutant X from the mother.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: How does consanguinity (cousin marriage) lead to the phenotypic expression of rare autosomal recessive disorders?
back: Increased Homozygosity. - Increases probability of both parents inheriting the same mutant allele. - Parents share a common ancestor. - Offspring inherit two copies of the recessive allele.

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: Distinguish between X-linked recessive and mitochondrial inheritance based on the offspring of an affected male.
back: X-linked Recessive: Affected male has carrier daughters and healthy sons. - Mitochondrial: Affected male has 100% healthy offspring (no transmission).

category: Describe the patterns of inheritance characteristic of autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X- linked dominant, X-linked recessive and mitochondrial traits
front: In medical genetics, identify the hallmark of 'vertical transmission' as seen in autosomal dominant pedigrees.
back: Multi-generational occurrence. - Trait appears in every generation. - Every affected person has at least one affected parent.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: In a standard medical pedigree, a square symbol uniquely represents a [___].
back:
* Male
* Standardized gender symbol used in genetic mapping.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A 4-year-old boy with suspected Thalassemia is the first family member evaluated. On a pedigree, he is marked with a small arrow. Identify this specific designation.
back:
* Proband (or Propositus)
* The index case that brings the family to medical attention.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Explain the visual representation and genetic implication of a double horizontal line connecting a male and a female in a pedigree.
back:
* Represents a consanguineous marriage (mating between relatives).
* Significantly increases the risk of autosomal recessive traits appearing in offspring.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: In a pedigree analysis, contrast the symbolic representation of monozygotic (identical) twins with dizygotic (fraternal) twins.
back:
* Monozygotic: Symbols originate from a single point and are connected by a horizontal bar.
* Dizygotic: Symbols originate from a single point but lack the horizontal connecting bar.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Identify the specific symbol used to denote a family member who is deceased.
back: * A diagonal line (slash) drawn through the individual's square or circle symbol.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: An individual who clinically expresses the phenotype of a genetic disease is represented by a [___] symbol.
back:
* Shaded (or filled-in)
* Used for both squares (males) and circles (females) to indicate affected status.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A pedigree for an autosomal recessive condition shows a circle that is only half-shaded. Describe the genotype and phenotype of this individual.
back:
* Genotype: Heterozygous (carrier).
* Phenotype: Clinically unaffected (normal).

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Describe the standardized system used to locate a specific person in a large pedigree (e.g., identifying individual 'III-2').
back:
* Roman Numerals: Indicate the generation level (top to bottom).
* Arabic Numerals: Indicate birth order or position within that generation (left to right).

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Distinguish the meaning of a circle with a central dot from a standard open circle in an X-linked recessive pedigree.
back:
* Central Dot: Represents an obligate carrier (heterozygous female).
* Open Circle: Represents a phenotypically normal female whose carrier status may be unknown.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Identify the symbol used to represent an individual whose sex is unknown or not specified (e.g., a fetus).
back: * A diamond shape.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: In a standard genetic pedigree, a square represents a [___] while a circle represents a [___].
back:
• Square: Denotes a male individual
• Circle: Denotes a female individual
• Unshaded symbols: Represent unaffected phenotypes
• Shaded symbols: Represent affected phenotypes

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A clinician investigates a family history of Hemophilia. The first affected individual brought to medical attention is indicated in the pedigree by an arrow. This person is termed the [___].
back:
• Proband: The index case (starting point)
• Propositus: The term for a male proband
• Proposita: The term for a female proband
• Represented by: A small arrow pointing to the symbol

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Explain the significance of a double horizontal line connecting a square and a circle in a genetic pedigree.
back:
• Consanguineous mating: Reproduction between related individuals (e.g., first cousins)
• Significance: Increases risk of autosomal recessive disorders
• Genetic impact: Higher probability of homozygous recessive offspring

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Contrast the visual representation of monozygotic twins with dizygotic twins in a standard pedigree chart.
back:
• Monozygotic: Two symbols branching from one point, connected by a horizontal bar
• Dizygotic: Two symbols branching from one point without a horizontal connector
• Significance: Identical vs. fraternal genetic contribution

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: How are generations and specific individuals within those generations standardly identified in a pedigree layout?
back:
• Generations: Marked with Roman numerals (I, II, III)
• Individuals: Numbered with Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3) from left to right
• Purpose: Allows precise localization of specific family members for genetic counseling

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A symbol with a diagonal slash drawn through it (e.g., a slashed square) indicates that the individual is [___].
back:
• Deceased: The individual has died
• Clinical importance: Helps establish age of onset and cause of death in familial conditions
• Phenotype: Shading inside the slashed symbol still indicates their disease status

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A pedigree for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy shows unshaded circles with a small central dot. Interpret this symbol and its clinical implication.
back:
• Obligate Carrier: Specifically for X-linked recessive traits
• Interpretation: The female is phenotypically normal but carries one mutant allele
• Risk: 50% chance of passing the mutant allele to sons

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Detail the interpretation of a small diamond-shaped symbol in a reproductive history pedigree.
back:
• Sex unspecified: Used for miscarriages, stillbirths, or abortions
• Interpretation: Often includes a number (e.g., '3') inside to indicate multiple losses
• Clinical utility: Identifies patterns of infertility or chromosomal lethalities

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Distinguish between a half-shaded symbol and a fully unshaded symbol in a pedigree suspected of Autosomal Recessive inheritance.
back:
• Half-shaded: Indicates a heterozygous carrier (clinically unaffected)
• Fully unshaded: Indicates an unaffected individual (either homozygous wild-type or carrier)
• Note: Shading half the symbol is optional and depends on known genotype data

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Identify the symbol used to denote a mating pair that is no longer together or is divorced.
back:
• Broken connector: A single horizontal line with a vertical break or double slash
• Utility: Clarifies lineage while acknowledging change in family structure
• Impact: Does not change the biological genetic descent shown

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: In a pedigree chart, a union between two closely related individuals (consanguineous mating) is represented by a [___] horizontal line connecting their symbols.
back: Double horizontal line.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A 5-year-old boy is the first family member to seek medical attention for a suspected hereditary disorder. His symbol on the family's pedigree is specifically indicated by a/an [___].
back: Arrow (pointing toward the symbol), identifying him as the proband, propositus, or index case.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Explain the standard alphanumeric system used to designate generations and individual birth order in a pedigree.
back: Generations are denoted by Roman numerals (I, II, III). Individuals within a generation are denoted by Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3) from left to right.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Contrast the symbolic representation of monozygotic (identical) twins with dizygotic (fraternal) twins.
back: Both arise from a single point; however, monozygotic twins are joined by an additional horizontal bar between their symbols, while dizygotic twins are not.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Identify the specific geometric symbol used to represent a family member whose sex is unknown or unspecified.
back: Diamond.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: An individual in a pedigree who has died is represented by a [___] through their square or circle.
back: Diagonal line.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A pedigree analysis shows that every shaded circle (mother) passes the trait to 100% of her offspring, regardless of sex, while shaded squares (fathers) have 0% affected offspring. This indicates [___] inheritance.
back: Mitochondrial (Maternal) inheritance.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Describe the symbolic marking used to denote an asymptomatic female carrier of an X-linked recessive trait.
back: A dot in the center of the circle, or a half-shaded circle.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Distinguish between a 'shaded' symbol and a 'half-shaded' symbol in the context of an autosomal recessive pedigree.
back: Shaded: Phenotypically affected (homozygous recessive). Half-shaded: Asymptomatic carrier (heterozygote).

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: State the basic geometric symbols utilized to differentiate biological males from females in medical genetics.
back: Male: Square. Female: Circle.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: In a standard genetic pedigree chart, a square that is completely filled or shaded represents an [___].
back:
• Affected male
• Indicates the individual manifests the specific phenotypic trait or genetic disease being tracked in the family tree.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: A pedigree for a family shows a horizontal line connecting a circle and a square, with a vertical line leading to a shaded circle. Identify the relationship and the clinical status of the child.
back:
• The horizontal line indicates mating/marriage.
• The shaded circle represents an affected daughter who expresses the genetic trait.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Explain the symbolic representation of a consanguineous marriage in a pedigree and its clinical significance in autosomal recessive inheritance.
back:
• Symbol: Two parallel horizontal lines connecting the related individuals.
• Significance: Increases risk of offspring inheriting rare recessive alleles from a shared common ancestor.

category: Interpret genetic symbols as they appear in pedigrees
front: Contrast the pedigree representation of monozygotic (identical) twins with that of dizygotic (fraternal) twins.
back:
