back: * Involves fusion of long arms of acrocentric chromosomes * Loss of short arms (p) occurs * Lost segments contain redundant rRNA genes, causing no clinical defect

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the clinical presentations and karyotypes of Down syndrome and Edwards syndrome.
back: * Down (Trisomy 21): Simian crease, flat facies, epicanthal folds * Edwards (Trisomy 18): Clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia * Karyotypes: 47,XX/XY,+21 vs 47,XX/XY,+18

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: State the clinical significance of identifying a 'balanced' versus 'unbalanced' structural chromosomal rearrangement in an asymptomatic parent.
back: * Balanced: No net loss/gain; parent is phenotypically normal * Unbalanced: Loss/gain of material; results in syndromes or miscarriage * Balanced carriers have high risk of producing unbalanced gametes

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The standard diagnostic laboratory tool used to visualize and count the full set of metaphase chromosomes for identifying aneuploidy is the [___].
back: * Karyotype * Requires cells arrested in metaphase (e.g., using colchicine) * Identifies numerical and large structural abnormalities

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A 35-year-old female experiences her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. Identify the most likely structural chromosomal abnormality present in one of the parents.
back: * Balanced Translocation (Reciprocal or Robertsonian) * Results in 'unbalanced' zygotes during meiotic segregation * Leads to non-viable pregnancies or congenital defects

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the mechanism of 'trisomy rescue' and its potential to cause uniparental disomy (UPD).
back: * Trisomic zygote loses one extra chromosome during early mitosis * If the two remaining chromosomes are from the same parent, UPD results * Can cause disorders like Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the genetic outcomes of nondisjunction occurring in Meiosis I versus Meiosis II regarding the inherited alleles.
back: * Meiosis I error: Two different homologs in one gamete (heterodisomy) * Meiosis II error: Two identical sister chromatids in one gamete (isodisomy) * Both result in aneuploidy post-fertilization

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: List the three autosomal trisomies that are viable enough to result in live births.
back: * Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) * Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) * Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A cell containing a total of 69 or 92 chromosomes, representing an exact multiple of the haploid set (n=23), is specifically termed [___].
back: Euploidy (specifically Polyploidy). 1. Triploidy (3n) and Tetraploidy (4n) are the most common forms. 2. Usually results from polyspermy or meiotic failure. 3. Almost always lethal in the prenatal or early neonatal period.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A neonate presents with a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single transverse palmar crease, and hypotonia. Identify the underlying numerical abnormality and its primary cause.
back: Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome). 1. Presence of three copies of chromosome 21. 2. Primarily caused by meiotic nondisjunction (95%). 3. Risk increases significantly with advanced maternal age.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast Robertsonian translocation with reciprocal translocation in terms of chromosome type and genetic material loss.
back: 1. Robertsonian: Occurs only in acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22); short arms (p) are lost. 2. Reciprocal: Segmental exchange between any chromosomes; usually balanced with no loss of material. 3. Both can produce unbalanced gametes.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A 17-year-old female with short stature and a webbed neck is compared to a 17-year-old male with tall stature, gynecomastia, and small testes. Contrast their chromosomal constitutions.
back: 1. Turner Syndrome: 45,X (monosomy X); female phenotype with streak ovaries. 2. Klinefelter Syndrome: 47,XXY; male phenotype with testicular atrophy. 3. Both are examples of sex chromosome aneuploidy resulting from nondisjunction.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: In the laboratory preparation of a clinical karyotype, identify the pharmacological agent added to the cell culture to arrest cells in metaphase by disrupting spindle fiber formation.
back: Colchicine. 1. Binds tubulin to inhibit microtubule polymerization. 2. Arrests the cell cycle at metaphase when chromosomes are most condensed. 3. Essential for clear visualization and structural analysis of the karyotype.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn with micrognathia, low-set ears, rocker-bottom feet, and clenched fists with the index finger overlapping the third finger likely has [___].
back: Trisomy 18 (Edwards Syndrome). 1. Second most common autosomal trisomy surviving to birth. 2. Characterized by severe intellectual disability and multisystem defects. 3. Highly associated with early neonatal mortality.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A child presents with a high-pitched, cat-like cry, microcephaly, and a moon-shaped face. This condition is caused by which specific structural chromosomal defect?
back: Chromosome 5p deletion. 1. Known as Cri-du-chat syndrome. 2. Results from the loss of a portion of the short arm (p) of chromosome 5. 3. Severity depends on the size of the deleted segment.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Differentiate between paracentric and pericentric inversions regarding their impact on the chromosomal centromere and gamete viability.
back: 1. Paracentric: Centromere is not involved; produces non-viable acentric or dicentric fragments. 2. Pericentric: Centromere is included; can produce balanced or unbalanced gametes with duplications/deletions. 3. Pericentric inversions can change the chromosome's arm ratio.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the chromosomal outcome of nondisjunction occurring in Meiosis I versus Meiosis II during gametogenesis.
back: 1. Meiosis I failure: Homologs fail to separate; results in gametes with both maternal and paternal homologs (heterodisomy). 2. Meiosis II failure: Sister chromatids fail to separate; results in gametes with two identical homologs (isodisomy).

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the structural chromosomal abnormality characterized by the presence of two identical arms (either two p-arms or two q-arms) due to horizontal centromere division.
back: Isochromosome. 1. Occurs when the centromere divides transversely rather than longitudinally. 2. Results in a chromosome with one arm deleted and the other duplicated. 3. Most common example is i(Xq) in Turner syndrome.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A chromosomal abnormality characterized by the gain or loss of one or more individual chromosomes (e.g., 45 or 47 instead of 46) is termed [___].
back:
• Aneuploidy
• Most commonly caused by meiotic nondisjunction
• Examples include Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome) and Monosomy X (Turner Syndrome).

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A phenotypically normal female is found to have 45 chromosomes, with one chromosome being a fusion of the long arms of 14 and 21. Identify the structural abnormality and the potential risk to her children.
back:
• Robertsonian Translocation
• Risk of Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21) in offspring due to unbalanced gamete formation
• The mother remains balanced and asymptomatic despite having 45 chromosomes.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the meiotic mechanism of nondisjunction and how it differs between Meiosis I and Meiosis II regarding the resulting gametes.
back:
• Failure of homologous chromosomes (Meiosis I) or sister chromatids (Meiosis II) to separate
• Meiosis I error: 100% abnormal gametes (disomic/nullisomic)
• Meiosis II error: 50% abnormal gametes.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast paracentric and pericentric inversions regarding the involvement of the centromere and the potential for changing the chromosome arm length ratio (p:q).
back:
• Pericentric: Involves the centromere; can alter arm length ratios
• Paracentric: Does not involve the centromere; arm lengths remain unchanged
• Both are balanced structural rearrangements.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Describe the mechanism of 'Mosaicism' and identify the stage of development where the causative error typically occurs.
back:
• Presence of two or more cell lines with different genotypes in one individual
• Caused by post-zygotic mitotic nondisjunction
• Results in variable clinical severity depending on cell distribution.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The presence of three complete sets of chromosomes (69,XXX or 69,XXY), usually resulting from double fertilization of an egg, is specifically termed [___].
back:
• Triploidy (a form of Polyploidy)
• Usually incompatible with life
• Distinguished from trisomy (which involves only one extra chromosome).

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A tall male presents with gynecomastia, azoospermia, and mild intellectual disability. Karyotype reveals 47,XXY. Identify the abnormality and the expected number of Barr bodies in his cells.
back:
• Klinefelter Syndrome
• Numerical abnormality (Sex chromosome trisomy)
• One Barr body present (due to X-inactivation of the extra X chromosome).

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the structural chromosomal error characterized by a chromosome having two identical arms (either two p-arms or two q-arms) and the division plane that creates it.
back:
• Isochromosome formation
• Caused by transverse (horizontal) division of the centromere instead of vertical/longitudinal
• Resulting cell is monosomic for one arm and trisomic for the other.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Distinguish between balanced reciprocal translocations and unbalanced translocations regarding the net change in genetic material and phenotypic outcomes.
back:
• Balanced: No net loss or gain of DNA; usually phenotypically normal but increased risk of miscarriages
• Unbalanced: Loss or gain of DNA; typically leads to severe congenital malformations.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the only human monosomy that is compatible with postnatal life and its typical chromosomal constitution.
back:
• Turner Syndrome
• 45,X (or 45,X0)
• Characteristics: Short stature, webbed neck, and streak ovaries.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The condition characterized by an abnormal number of chromosomes that is not an exact multiple of the haploid set (e.g., 45 or 47 chromosomes) is termed [___].
back:
Aneuploidy
- Results from nondisjunction during meiosis or mitosis.
- Common examples include trisomy (2n+1) and monosomy (2n-1).

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A phenotypically normal male has a karyotype showing a fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (14 and 21), with the loss of their short arms. Identify the structural abnormality and its clinical significance for his offspring.
back:
Robertsonian Translocation
- The individual is a balanced carrier.
- High risk of producing gametes leading to Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome) in offspring.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the role of post-zygotic mitotic errors in the development of chromosomal mosaicism.
back:
Mosaicism Mechanism
- Occurs after fertilization during early mitotic divisions.
- Results in two or more genetically distinct cell lines within one individual.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the genomic outcomes of a balanced reciprocal translocation with an unbalanced translocation in terms of phenotype and offspring risk.
back:
Balanced vs. Unbalanced Translocations
- Balanced: No net loss/gain; usually normal phenotype; high risk for abnormal offspring.
- Unbalanced: Significant DNA gain/loss; usually results in severe phenotypic defects or lethality.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the structural chromosomal abnormality where a segment of a chromosome is rotated 180 degrees and reinserted without including the centromere.
back:
Paracentric Inversion
- Does not involve the centromere.
- Usually balanced in the individual but can lead to non-viable, acentric, or dicentric gametes.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: In the context of numerical abnormalities, the presence of three complete sets of chromosomes (3n = 69) is specifically called [___].
back:
Triploidy
- A form of polyploidy.
- Most commonly caused by dispermy (fertilization of an egg by two sperm).

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A fetus is diagnosed with a partial loss of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). Identify the structural abnormality type and the likely clinical presentation.
back:
Terminal Deletion
- Results in Cri-du-chat syndrome.
- Characterized by microcephaly, intellectual disability, and a high-pitched cat-like cry.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Describe the primary mechanism of meiotic nondisjunction and distinguish its effects when occurring in Meiosis I versus Meiosis II.
back:
Nondisjunction
- Meiosis I: Failure of homologous chromosomes to separate; results in 100% abnormal gametes.
- Meiosis II: Failure of sister chromatids to separate; results in 50% abnormal gametes.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the formation of a ring chromosome with the formation of an isochromosome.
back:
Structural Variation
- Ring: Formed by two terminal deletions and fusion of the 'sticky' ends.
- Isochromosome: Formed by horizontal (transverse) rather than longitudinal division of the centromere.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the chromosomal abnormality that involves the exchange of segments between non-homologous chromosomes where the total chromosome number remains 46.
back:
Reciprocal Translocation
- Genetic material is traded between two different chromosomes.
- Often detected via karyotyping or FISH if the segments are large enough.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: An individual possessing an entire extra set of chromosomes (e.g., 3n = 69) is described as having the numerical abnormality called [___].
back:
- Polyploidy
- Characterized by multiples of the haploid number (n)
- Triploidy (3n) and Tetraploidy (4n) are typically incompatible with life

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A neonate presents with a flat facial profile, epicanthic folds, and a single transverse palmar crease. Karyotype shows 47,XX,+21. Identify the numerical abnormality and its most common cause.
back:
- Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome)
- Most common autosomal aneuploidy
- Primarily caused by maternal meiotic nondisjunction

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the cellular mechanism of nondisjunction and its effect on the resulting gametes.
back:
- Failure of chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis
- Leads to gametes with n+1 or n-1 chromosomes
- Results in aneuploid zygotes (trisomy or monosomy)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast Paracentric and Pericentric inversions regarding the involvement of the centromere.
back:
- Pericentric: Involves two breaks in opposite arms and includes the centromere
- Paracentric: Involves two breaks in the same arm; does not include the centromere

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Summarize the structural rearrangement involved in a Robertsonian translocation.
back:
- Fusion of two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 14 and 21) at the centromere
- Loss of short arms (p-arms) containing redundant rRNA genes
- Carriers have 45 chromosomes but are phenotypically normal

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The condition where an individual has two or more cell lines with different karyotypes (e.g., some cells 46,XX and others 45,X) is [___].
back:
- Mosaicism
- Usually results from mitotic nondisjunction after fertilization
- Clinical severity depends on the percentage of abnormal cells

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A tall male presents with infertility, small firm testes, and gynecomastia. Karyotype reveals 47,XXY. Identify the syndrome and the chromosomal defect.
back:
- Klinefelter Syndrome
- Numerical sex chromosome abnormality (trisomy)
- Presence of an extra X chromosome in a male

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: How does a reciprocal translocation differ from a chromosomal insertion in terms of genetic exchange?
back:
- Reciprocal: Two-way exchange of segments between non-homologous chromosomes
- Insertion: One-way movement of a segment into a different chromosome
- Reciprocal is a mutual exchange; insertion is not

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Distinguish between Monosomy and Trisomy in the context of human aneuploidy.
back:
- Monosomy: Loss of a single chromosome (2n-1); e.g., Turner Syndrome
- Trisomy: Gain of an extra chromosome (2n+1); e.g., Patau Syndrome (Trisomy 13)
- Monosomies are generally more lethal than trisomies

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the chromosomal abnormality in a female presenting with short stature, webbed neck, and primary amenorrhea.
back:
- Turner Syndrome (45,X)
- Characterized by X-chromosome monosomy
- Only viable human monosomy

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell, such as having 45 or 47 instead of the standard 46, is defined as [___].
back:
- Aneuploidy
 - Usually results from nondisjunction during meiosis
 - Includes trisomies (gain) and monosomies (loss)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn presents with a flat facial profile, hypotonia, and a single palmar crease. Karyotyping confirms an extra copy of chromosome 21. Identify the numerical abnormality and its most common etiology.
back:
- Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome)
 - Caused by meiotic nondisjunction
 - Risk increases with advanced maternal age

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the structural mechanism behind a Robertsonian translocation involving acrocentric chromosomes.
back:
- Long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at the centromere
 - Short arms are lost, usually without phenotypic effect
 - Reduces total chromosome count to 45 in balanced carriers

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast aneuploidy with polyploidy regarding the magnitude of chromosomal change.
back:
- Aneuploidy: Loss or gain of single chromosomes (e.g., 2n+1)
 - Polyploidy: Addition of entire haploid sets (e.g., 3n, 4n)
 - Polyploidy is generally incompatible with human life

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Distinguish between pericentric and paracentric chromosomal inversions.
back:
- Pericentric: Inversion segment includes the centromere
 - Paracentric: Inversion is confined to one arm, excluding the centromere
 - Both involve two breaks in one chromosome followed by 180-degree rotation

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A structural abnormality resulting in the loss of a chromosomal segment, often identified in the ΔF508 mutation of the CFTR gene, is termed a [___].
back:
- Deletion
 - Results in partial monosomy for the lost region
 - Can be interstitial (internal) or terminal (end of arm)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A patient is identified as having two distinct cell populations: one with 46,XX and another with 45,X. Identify the biological term for this finding and its timing in development.
back:
- Chromosomal Mosaicism
 - Occurs post-zygotic (after fertilization)
 - Caused by mitotic nondisjunction during early cleavage

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Analyze how nondisjunction in Meiosis I differs from Meiosis II regarding the inheritance of parental homologs.
back:
- Meiosis I: Gamete inherits both parental homologs (different alleles)
 - Meiosis II: Gamete inherits two copies of a single parental homolog (identical alleles)
 - Both lead to aneuploid offspring

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the clinical phenotype of balanced translocations with unbalanced translocations.
back:
- Balanced: Phenotypically normal (no gain/loss of DNA); risk of abnormal offspring
 - Unbalanced: Phenotypically abnormal due to net loss or gain of genetic material
 - Leads to partial monosomy or partial trisomy

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the standard diagnostic method used to evaluate an individual's chromosomal number and major structural morphology during metaphase.
back:
- Karyotyping
 - Uses G-banding (Giemsa stain)
 - Visualizes chromosomal size, centromere position, and banding patterns

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The condition characterized by a numerical chromosomal abnormality where the number of chromosomes is not an exact multiple of the haploid set (23) is termed [___].
back:
* Aneuploidy
* Usually results from meiotic nondisjunction
* Includes trisomy (extra chromosome) and monosomy (missing chromosome)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn presents with hypotonia, a flat occiput, epicanthal folds, and a single transverse palmar crease. Karyotype analysis confirms an extra copy of chromosome 21. Identify the numerical abnormality and its most significant risk factor.
back:
* Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome)
* Advanced maternal age (increased risk of meiotic nondisjunction)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the mechanism and structural outcome of a chromosomal inversion.
back:
* Two breaks occur in a single chromosome
* The segment between breaks rotates 180 degrees and reinserts
* Genetic material is balanced but gene order is reversed

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A phenotypic woman with a history of recurrent miscarriages is found to have a 45,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10) karyotype. Contrast the clinical implications of her 'balanced' status with the potential 'unbalanced' outcomes in her offspring.
back:
* Balanced: Individual has full genetic complement; phenotypically normal.
* Unbalanced Offspring: May inherit extra/missing segments, leading to conditions like translocation Down Syndrome.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Define the chromosomal phenomenon known as 'Mosaicism' and identify its typical cause.
back:
* Presence of two or more cell lines with different genotypes in one individual
* Caused by mitotic nondisjunction occurring after zygote formation

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during cell division is called [___], which is the primary cause of numerical abnormalities.
back:
* Nondisjunction
* Occurs in Meiosis I (homologues) or Meiosis II/Mitosis (sister chromatids)
* Leads to aneuploid gametes (n+1 or n-1)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A 16-year-old male is evaluated for small testes, gynecomastia, and sparse body hair. Karyotype shows 47,XXY. Identify the syndrome and the specific numerical chromosomal classification.
back:
* Klinefelter Syndrome
* Sex chromosome aneuploidy (Trisomy)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Discuss the structural formation of a Robertsonian Translocation and identify the specific chromosome types involved.
back:
* Fusion of the long arms (q) of two acrocentric chromosomes
* Short arms (p) are lost; chromosome count reduces to 45
* Involves chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the effects on the chromosomal arm ratio (p:q) between paracentric and pericentric inversions.
back:
* Paracentric: Centromere is not involved; no change in arm ratio.
* Pericentric: Centromere is included in the inversion; often changes the arm ratio.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the numerical abnormality characterized by a chromosomal count that is an exact multiple of the haploid set (e.g., 69 or 92 chromosomes) but exceeds the diploid number.
back:
* Polyploidy
* Includes triploidy (3n = 69) and tetraploidy (4n = 92)
* Usually results from polyspermy or failure of meiotic maturation

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human somatic cell contains a diploid (2n) number of [___] chromosomes.
back: 46 chromosomes (organized as 23 pairs).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A newborn presents with a flat nasal bridge, upslanting palpebral fissures, and a single transverse palmar crease. A karyotype of this infant would most likely reveal [___].
back: Trisomy 21 (47, XX/XY, +21).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain the biological importance of utilizing metaphase-stage cells for clinical karyotyping.
back: Chromosomes are in their most condensed state. Sister chromatids are clearly visible. Allows for accurate identification of number and structure.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the structural arrangement of a metacentric chromosome with that of an acrocentric chromosome.
back: Metacentric: Centromere is centrally located; p and q arms are roughly equal. Acrocentric: Centromere is near one end; p-arm is extremely short (satellites); q-arm is long.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Define the anatomical distinction between the 'p-arm' and 'q-arm' of a human chromosome.
back: p-arm: Short arm (from French 'petit'). q-arm: Long arm. Separated by the centromere.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: The standardized procedure of staining metaphase chromosomes to produce characteristic light and dark patterns for identifying homologues is known as [___].
back: G-banding (Giemsa staining).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A phenotypically normal male is found to have a karyotype of 45,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10). Identify the specific structural abnormality and the risk to his offspring.
back: Robertsonian translocation. Increased risk of Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21) in offspring via unbalanced gametes.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe the functional components of a chromosome that ensure structural integrity during the cell cycle and prevent nuclease degradation.
back: Telomeres (hexameric repeats at ends). Centromere (kinetochore attachment site). DNA-histone (nucleosome) complex.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between the chromosomal composition of an autosome and an allosome in a normal human karyotype.
back: Autosomes: Pairs 1–22; determine non-sex traits. Allosomes: Pair 23 (X and Y); determine biological sex.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the total number of chromosomes found in a normal human haploid (n) set.
back: 23 chromosomes (22 autosomes + 1 sex chromosome).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human somatic cell contains a total of [___] chromosomes, consisting of 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.
back:
• 46
• Arranged as 23 pairs
• Diploid (2n) state

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A 28-year-old male undergoes fertility testing. The cytogenetics report identifies a normal male chromosome complement. State the standard ISCN notation for this finding.
back:
• 46,XY
• Indicates 46 total chromosomes
• XY sex chromosome constitution

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain the role of colchicine in the laboratory preparation of a human karyotype from a peripheral blood sample.
back:
• Inhibits spindle fiber formation
• Arrests cells in metaphase
• Ensures maximum chromosome condensation for visualization

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the structure of acrocentric chromosomes with metacentric chromosomes in a human karyotype.
back:
• Metacentric: Centromere in the middle; p and q arms roughly equal
• Acrocentric: Centromere near one end; very short p arms often featuring satellites

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the specific phase of the cell cycle where chromosomes are most highly condensed and traditionally visualized for karyotyping.
back:
• Metaphase
• Chromosomes consist of two sister chromatids
• Joined at the centromere

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: In human cytogenetics, the shorter arm of a chromosome is designated as the [___] arm, while the longer arm is designated as the [___] arm.
back:
• p (petite)
• q (following 'p' in the alphabet)

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A lab technician observes dark bands on a Giemsa-stained (G-banded) chromosome. Describe the biochemical significance of these dark bands.
back:
• Represent AT-rich DNA
• Gene-poor regions
• Late-replicating heterochromatin

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe how telomeres maintain the structural integrity of human chromosomes during replication.
back:
• Capping: Prevents nuclease attack
• Distinction: Prevents repair systems from mistaking ends for DSB breaks
• T-loop formation: Stabilized by shelterin proteins

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between haploid and diploid chromosome numbers in the context of human gametes and somatic cells.
back:
• Diploid (2n): 46 chromosomes (somatic cells)
• Haploid (n): 23 chromosomes (sperm/ova)

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the five specific pairs of autosomes in a normal human karyotype that are classified as acrocentric.
back:
• Pairs 13, 14, 15 (Group D)
• Pairs 21, 22 (Group G)
• Often contain nucleolar organizer regions (NORs)

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: The normal human somatic cell contains a diploid number of [___] chromosomes.
back:
• 46 chromosomes.
• Arranged in 23 pairs.
• Consists of 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A phenotypic male patient undergoes genetic testing. The laboratory report indicates a 46,XY karyotype. Interpret the structural significance of the 'Y' chromosome in this result.
back:
• Contains the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region Y).
• Triggers male sexual differentiation.
• Smaller than the X chromosome and contains fewer genes.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain the structural roles of the 'p' and 'q' arms when describing human chromosomal anatomy.
back:
• p-arm: The short arm (from 'petite').
• q-arm: The long arm.
• They are separated by the centromere, which acts as the primary constriction site.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the centromere placement in submetacentric versus acrocentric chromosomes found in a human karyotype.
back:
• Submetacentric: Centromere is off-center, creating distinct short and long arms.
• Acrocentric: Centromere is near the very end; p-arm is tiny, often containing stalks/satellites.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the genetic terminology used to describe the set of 23 chromosomes found in human sperm or ova.
back:
• Haploid number (n).
• Contains one member of each autosome pair and one sex chromosome.
• Formed via meiosis to ensure diploidy upon fertilization.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: During karyotype preparation, the chemical colchicine is used to arrest cells in [___], the stage where chromosomes are most condensed and visible.
back:
• Metaphase (of mitosis).
• Chromosomes consist of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
• Maximum coiling allows for clear identification of banding patterns.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A karyotype shows a 45,X notation. Based on the standard human chromosome number, deduce the clinical significance of this finding.
back:
• Turner Syndrome.
• Aneuploidy (monosomy X).
• Missing one sex chromosome, resulting in a total of 45 chromosomes instead of 46.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain how G-banding (Giemsa staining) enables the structural interpretation of specific chromosome regions.
back:
• Produces unique dark (AT-rich, gene-poor) and light (GC-rich, gene-rich) bands.
• Allows for identification of individual pairs.
• Facilitates detection of structural deletions, translocations, or inversions.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between autosomes and sex chromosomes within the 46-chromosome human complement.
back:
• Autosomes: Pairs 1–22; determine non-sex-linked physical traits.
• Sex Chromosomes: 23rd pair (XX or XY); determine biological sex and primary sexual characteristics.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: What structural component at the ends of human chromosomes prevents DNA degradation and end-to-end fusion?
back:
• Telomeres.
• Repetitive DNA sequences (TTAGGG).
• Associated with shelterin proteins.
• Shorten with each cell division in somatic cells.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human somatic cell contains 46 chromosomes, where 44 are categorized as [___] and 2 are sex chromosomes.
back:
Autosomes. 
- Consist of 22 pairs.
- Carry non-sex determining genetic information.
- Identical in both males and females.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A cytogeneticist analyzes a skin fibroblast culture and identifies a karyotype of 46,XX. Interpret this finding in the context of biological sex and chromosome count.
back:
- Normal female karyotype.
- Diploid (2n) state.
- 46 total chromosomes.
- Two X chromosomes present with 44 autosomes.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain how the drug colchicine is utilized during the preparation of a sample for karyotype analysis.
back:
- Inhibits spindle formation (microtubules).
- Arrests cells in metaphase.
- Ensures maximum chromosome condensation for visualization.
- Facilitates clear identification of banding patterns.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the structure of an acrocentric chromosome with that of a metacentric chromosome as seen on a karyogram.
back:
- Metacentric: Centromere is central; p and q arms are equal length.
- Acrocentric: Centromere near one end; p arm is extremely short (satellites), q arm is long.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe the conventional alphanumeric notation used to designate a specific location on the short arm of chromosome 7.
back:
- Uses prefix "7p".
- "7" represents the chromosome number.
- "p" (petit) denotes the short arm.
- Followed by region/band numbers (e.g., 7p21).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Human gametes (sperm and ova) contain a [___] number of chromosomes, totaling 23.
back:
Haploid (n).
- One set of 23 chromosomes.
- Result of meiosis.
- Combines with another gamete to restore diploidy.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia undergoes karyotyping. The report shows "46,XY". Identify the specific chromosome structure that determines male biological development in this instance.
back:
- Y chromosome.
- Specifically the SRY gene.
- Directs testes development.
- Presence of 44 autosomes in diploid set.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe the structural components of a chromosome that are visualized using Giemsa staining (G-banding) in a standard karyotype.
back:
- Dark bands: AT-rich, gene-poor, late-replicating.
- Light bands: GC-rich, gene-dense, early-replicating.
- Allows identification of p/q arms and centromeres.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between the "p" and "q" arms of a human chromosome in terms of size and nomenclature.
back:
- p arm: Short arm (French "petit").
- q arm: Long arm (alphabetically follows p).
- Separated by the centromere.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the specialized DNA-protein complexes at the extreme ends of chromosomes that maintain structural integrity during replication.
back:
Telomeres.
- Hexameric repeats (TTAGGG).
- Prevent end-to-end fusion.
- Protect against DNA degradation during mitosis.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human somatic cell contains a total of [___] chromosomes, representing the diploid (2n) state.
back:
46 chromosomes
- Organized as 22 pairs of autosomes
- 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY)
- Totaling 23 homologous pairs

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A 37-year-old female undergoes amniocentesis to screen for fetal aneuploidy. The laboratory procedure that visualizes metaphase chromosomes to assess their number and morphology is known as [___].
back:
Karyotyping
- Assesses chromosome size and banding
- Identifies numerical abnormalities (e.g., trisomy)
- Detects structural defects (e.g., translocations)

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain the structural composition of a nucleosome 'bead' within the eukaryotic chromosome.
back:
- DNA segment (approx. 147 bp)
- Wrapped nearly twice around a core
- Histone Octamer: 2 molecules each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the chromosome number between human somatic cells and mature germ cells (gametes).
back:
- Somatic Cells: Diploid (46 chromosomes)
- Germ Cells: Haploid (23 chromosomes)
- Haploid set contains one of each autosome and one sex chromosome

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the specific stage of the cell cycle where chromosomes are most condensed and typically harvested for karyotyping.
back:
Metaphase
- DNA is highly coiled
- Sister chromatids are clearly visible
- Standardized staining (G-banding) is performed here

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: In the structural hierarchy of a chromosome, the specialized histone that binds to 'linker DNA' to facilitate higher-level packing is [___].
back:
Histone H1
- Binds the DNA between nucleosomes
- Stabilizes the 30-nm nucleofilament
- Most species-specific and tissue-specific histone

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A newborn presents with hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, and a single palmar crease. Karyotypic analysis shows 47,XY,+21. Describe the structural nature of this abnormality.
back:
Numerical Aneuploidy (Trisomy 21)
- Presence of an extra autosome
- Total chromosome count is 47
- Caused by meiotic non-disjunction

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe the chemical interactions that allow histones to bind tightly to the DNA molecule.
back:
- Histones: Positively charged (rich in Lysine/Arginine)
- DNA: Negatively charged (Phosphate backbone)
- Strong ionic bonds facilitate tight coiling

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between the karyotypic notations for a normal human male versus a normal human female.
back:
- Male: 46,XY
- Female: 46,XX
- Notation indicates total number and sex chromosome complement

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Define 'Chromatin' as it exists within the eukaryotic nucleus.
back:
- Complex of DNA and proteins
- Proteins: Histones and non-histone proteins
- Forms the substance of eukaryotic chromosomes

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: In medical genetics, a numerical abnormality characterized by a chromosome number that is not an exact multiple of the haploid set (23) is specifically termed [___].
back:
Aneuploidy.
- Commonly results from meiotic nondisjunction.
- Includes monosomy (2n-1) and trisomy (2n+1).
- Clinical examples: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21) and Turner Syndrome (45,X).

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A tall, 32-year-old male presents with infertility, small firm testes, and gynecomastia. Cytogenetic analysis reveals a 47,XXY karyotype. Identify the most common underlying cellular mechanism.
back:
Meiotic Nondisjunction.
- Failure of homologous chromosomes (Meiosis I) or sister chromatids (Meiosis II) to separate.
- Results in Klinefelter syndrome.
- Risk increases significantly with advanced maternal age.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Describe the structural mechanism that leads to the formation of a Robertsonian translocation.
back:
Centric Fusion.
- Occurs between two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22).
- Involves the loss of short arms (p-arms) and fusion of long arms (q-arms).
- Resulting chromosome contains nearly all functional genetic material.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the cytogenetic features and centromeric involvement of paracentric inversions versus pericentric inversions.
back:
- Paracentric: Two breaks occur in a single arm; does NOT involve the centromere.
- Pericentric: One break in each arm; DOES involve the centromere.
- Pericentric inversions may change the p:q arm ratio.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the term 'Mosaicism' as it pertains to clinical chromosomal abnormalities.
back:
- Presence of two or more genetically different cell lines in one individual.
- All cell lines derived from a single zygote.
- Caused by mitotic nondisjunction during post-zygotic early embryonic development.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The structural abnormality where a chromosome loses both distal ends, which then fuse to form a circular structure, is termed a [___] chromosome.
back:
Ring Chromosome.
- Results from double terminal deletions in both p and q arms.
- Leads to loss of telomeric genetic material.
- Usually unstable during subsequent mitoses.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn girl presents with lymphedema of the hands, a webbed neck, and widely spaced nipples. Identify the expected chromosomal abnormality and its shorthand notation.
back:
Turner Syndrome (45,X).
- Represents X-chromosome monosomy.
- Most common cause of primary amenorrhea.
- Associated with streak ovaries and coarctation of the aorta.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the mechanical error during cell division that results in 'isochromosome' formation.
back:
Transverse Centromere Division.
- Centromere divides horizontally instead of longitudinally.
- Results in a chromosome with two identical arms (p or q).
- Leads to partial monosomy of one arm and partial trisomy of the other.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Distinguish between Balanced and Unbalanced translocations in terms of clinical phenotype.
back:
- Balanced: No net gain or loss of genetic material; usually phenotypically normal.
- Unbalanced: Net gain or loss of DNA; results in clinical abnormalities or lethality.
- Balanced carriers have high risk for producing unbalanced gametes.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the specific chromosomal abnormality resulting from a terminal deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-).
back:
Cri-du-Chat Syndrome.
- Named for characteristic cat-like cry in infancy.
- Associated with microcephaly and severe intellectual disability.
- Classic example of a partial deletion syndrome.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A condition characterized by an abnormal number of chromosomes that is not an exact multiple of the haploid set (e.g., 45 or 47 chromosomes) is termed [___].
back:
* Aneuploidy
* Most commonly caused by nondisjunction
* Examples include monosomy and trisomy

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn presents with dysmorphic features. Karyotyping reveals the fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (e.g., 14 and 21) with the loss of their short arms. Identify this structural abnormality.
back:
* Robertsonian Translocation
* Occurs only in acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22)
* Carrier is phenotypically normal but at risk for unbalanced offspring

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the mechanism by which an individual develops mosaicism, where different cell lines have different chromosomal constitutions.
back:
* Mitotic nondisjunction
* Occurs after fertilization (post-zygotic stage)
* Results in a mixture of normal and aneuploid cells in the same individual

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the structural implications of a pericentric inversion with a paracentric inversion in human chromosomes.
back:
* Pericentric: Involves the centromere; can change the arm length ratio (p/q)
* Paracentric: Does not involve the centromere; arm ratio remains unchanged
* Both involve two breaks in a single chromosome followed by 180-degree rotation

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the pharmacological agent used in cytogenetics to arrest cells in metaphase by inhibiting microtubule polymerization for chromosomal analysis.
back:
* Colchicine (or Colcemid)
* Inhibits spindle fiber formation
* Ensures chromosomes are at their most condensed state for karyotyping

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: In structural chromosomal abnormalities, an [___] is formed when the centromere divides horizontally instead of vertically, resulting in two identical arms.
back:
* Isochromosome
* Results in monosomy for one arm and trisomy for the other
* Frequently seen in the X chromosome (Turner syndrome variants)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A 35-year-old female undergoes amniocentesis. The results show a 47,XX,+21 karyotype. Describe the primary biological event during gametogenesis that led to this numerical abnormality.
back:
* Meiotic Nondisjunction
* Failure of homologous chromosomes (Meiosis I) or sister chromatids (Meiosis II) to separate
* Risk increases significantly with advanced maternal age

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Differentiate the molecular impact of a balanced translocation from an unbalanced translocation regarding phenotypic expression.
back:
* Balanced: No loss or gain of genetic material; usually phenotypically normal
* Unbalanced: Significant loss or gain of DNA; typically leads to severe clinical defects or fetal demise
* Balanced carriers often present with recurrent miscarriages

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast the genomic consequences of polyploidy with aneuploidy in human development.
back:
* Polyploidy: Gain of entire sets of chromosomes (e.g., 3n = 69); usually lethal
* Aneuploidy: Gain or loss of a single chromosome (e.g., 2n+1); may be compatible with life
* Polyploidy often results from dispermy

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: List the two fundamental categories of chromosomal mutations and specify the type that involves a 180-degree reversal of a chromosome segment.
back:
* Categories: Numerical and Structural
* Reversal Type: Inversion
* Inversions are usually balanced but can cause gamete imbalances

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human somatic cell contains [___] pairs of autosomes and [___] pair of sex chromosomes.
back:
• 22 pairs of autosomes.
• 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY).
• Total of 46 chromosomes (diploid).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A cytogeneticist reviews a metaphase spread and observes a 46,XY karyotype. Interpret the clinical significance of this finding.
back:
• Represents a normal male.
• 46 chromosomes total.
• Presence of Y chromosome determines male sex.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain the role of colchicine in the preparation of a human karyotype.
back:
• Inhibits spindle fiber formation.
• Arrests cells in metaphase.
• Maximizes chromosome condensation for clear visualization.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A 25-year-old female undergoes genetic screening. Her report shows a 46,XX result. Contrast the chromosomal composition of her somatic cells versus her gametes.
back:
• Somatic: Diploid (2n), 46 chromosomes.
• Gametes: Haploid (n), 23 chromosomes.
• Gametes contain only one sex chromosome (X).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Differentiate between the 'p' and 'q' arms of a human chromosome.
back:
• p-arm: Short arm (from 'petite').
• q-arm: Long arm.
• Separated by the centromere.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A chromosome with a centromere placed so that one arm is significantly shorter than the other is termed [___].
back:
• Submetacentric.
• Note: Metacentric has equal arms; Acrocentric has centromeres near the end.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A laboratory analysis reveals a chromosome with the centromere located at the very end, with p-arms appearing as small satellites. Identify the morphological class.
back:
• Acrocentric.
• In humans, includes chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: How does Giemsa staining (G-banding) facilitate the interpretation of a normal karyotype?
back:
• Creates unique light and dark band patterns.
• Allows identification of homologous pairs.
• Facilitates detection of structural deletions or translocations.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between metacentric and telocentric chromosomes in the context of human cytogenetics.
back:
• Metacentric: Centromere in middle; equal arms.
• Telocentric: Centromere at the tip.
• Note: Telocentric chromosomes do not occur in humans.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the repetitive DNA sequences located at the terminal ends of a normal human chromosome.
back:
• Telomeres.
• Consist of TTAGGG hexameric repeats.
• Protect chromosome ends from degradation and fusion.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human somatic cell contains a diploid number of chromosomes, specifically [___] individual chromosomes.
back:
46 chromosomes.
Arranged as 23 pairs.
Includes 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A lab report for a healthy male neonate displays a karyotype of 46,XY. Interpret the 'XY' component of this notation in terms of genetic sex.
back:
Represents the sex chromosomes.
Indicates a male phenotype.
X is from the mother, Y is from the father.
Y contains the SRY gene for testis development.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe the categorization of chromosomes based on centromere position during karyotype analysis.
back:
Metacentric: Centromere in middle (equal arms).
Submetacentric: Centromere off-center (short p-arm, long q-arm).
Acrocentric: Centromere near one end (satellite/stalks present).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the 'p' and 'q' designations used in describing the structure of a human chromosome.
back:
p-arm: Refers to the short arm (from 'petit').
q-arm: Refers to the long arm.
Separated by the centromere; used for gene locus mapping.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Specify the mitotic phase where cells are typically arrested for chromosomal visualization in a karyotype and the agent used.
back:
Metaphase.
Chromosomes are most condensed.
Colchicine or Vinblastine is used to inhibit spindle formation and arrest the cycle.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Human gametes (sperm and ova) contain a [___] number of chromosomes, totaling 23.
back:
Haploid (n).
Result of meiotic reduction division.
Restores diploidy (2n=46) upon fertilization.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A 46,XX karyotype is observed. Upon Giemsa staining (G-banding), specify what the resulting light and dark bands represent.
back:
Dark bands: AT-rich, gene-poor regions.
Light bands: GC-rich, gene-dense regions.
Unique banding patterns allow for individual chromosome identification.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain the role of telomeres located at the distal ends of a normal human chromosome.
back:
Repetitive DNA sequences (TTAGGG).
Caps chromosome ends to prevent degradation or fusion.
Maintains structural stability and serves as a 'mitotic clock'.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between autosomes and sex chromosomes in the context of a normal human karyotype.
back:
Autosomes: Pairs 1-22; identical in both sexes; code for somatic traits.
Sex Chromosomes: Pair 23; XX (female) or XY (male); determine sexual differentiation.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the specific chromosome pairs in a human karyotype that are acrocentric and often possess satellites.
back:
Pairs 13, 14, 15 (D group).
Pairs 21, 22 (G group).
Often involved in Robertsonian translocations due to their structure.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human somatic cell contains a total of [___] chromosomes, consisting of 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes.
back:
• 46 chromosomes (diploid number).
• 44 autosomes.
• 2 sex chromosomes (XX or XY).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A laboratory report for a phenotypic male indicates a '46,XY' result. Interpret the components of this standard notation.
back:
• 46: Total chromosome count.
• XY: Sex chromosome complement (Male).
• Implies 22 pairs of homologous autosomes.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: During the preparation of a karyotype, explain why cells are treated with colchicine before staining.
back:
• Arrests cells in metaphase.
• Inhibits spindle fiber formation.
• Ensures maximum condensation of chromosomes for visualization.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the structure of metacentric chromosomes with acrocentric chromosomes based on centromere position.
back:
• Metacentric: Centromere in middle; arms roughly equal.
• Acrocentric: Centromere near one end; very small p-arms (satellites).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the structural convention used to differentiate the 'p' and 'q' arms of a chromosome.
back:
• p-arm: Short arm (petit).
• q-arm: Long arm.
• Divided by the centromere (primary constriction).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: The most common diagnostic technique used to produce characteristic light and dark bands for identifying individual chromosome pairs is [___] staining.
back:
• G-banding (Giemsa staining).
• Dark bands: A-T rich, gene-poor regions.
• Light bands: G-C rich, gene-active regions.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A 25-year-old female's genetic screening reveals a '46,XX' constitution. Define the chromosomal count and arrangement present in her somatic cells.
back:
• 46 total (2n) chromosomes.
• 44 autosomes arranged in 22 pairs.
• Two homologous X chromosomes.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe how chromosomes are systematically ordered from 1 to 22 in a standard human karyogram.
back:
• Decreasing size/length.
• Position of the centromere.
• Unique banding patterns (G-bands).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between the chromosomal status of a human gamete versus a human somatic cell.
back:
• Gamete: Haploid (n=23); one set of chromosomes.
• Somatic: Diploid (2n=46); two homologous sets.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Specify the role of the centromere in chromosomal classification and cell division.
back:
• Primary constriction dividing p and q arms.
• Site of kinetochore formation.
• Attachment point for spindle microtubules.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: The short arm of a chromosome in a human karyotype is designated as the [___] arm.
back:
• 'p' arm (from the French 'petit').
• Represents the segment above the centromere.
• Used in cytogenetic mapping to locate specific genes.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Cytogenetic analysis of a neonate with a flat facial profile and simian crease reveals a 47,XY,+21 karyotype. This numerical abnormality is specifically termed [___].
back:
• Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome).
• An example of autosomal aneuploidy.
• Caused by meiotic non-disjunction, resulting in an extra chromosome 21.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain why cells are typically arrested in metaphase using spindle poisons like colchicine for karyotypic analysis.
back:
• Chromosomes are at their most condensed state.
• Sister chromatids are clearly visible and distinguishable.
• Spindle poisons inhibit microtubule polymerization, preventing anaphase separation.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the centromeric position and structural components of metacentric chromosomes with acrocentric chromosomes.
back:
• Metacentric: Centromere is central; p and q arms are roughly equal length.
• Acrocentric: Centromere near one end; p arm is minute, often possessing satellites/stalks for rRNA synthesis.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between the haploid and diploid number of chromosomes in a normal human lifecycle.
back:
• Haploid (n): 23 chromosomes; characteristic of gametes (sperm/ova).
• Diploid (2n): 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); characteristic of somatic cells.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A normal human female karyotype is represented by the standard clinical notation [___].
back:
• 46,XX.
• Indicates 46 total chromosomes with two X sex chromosomes.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A phenotypically normal female has 45 chromosomes, including a fusion of the long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21. Identify this specific structural rearrangement.
back:
• Robertsonian Translocation.
• Occurs between acrocentric chromosomes.
• Loss of the short (p) arms is clinically negligible in the carrier but increases risk of Down Syndrome in offspring.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Describe the mechanism by which Giemsa staining (G-banding) facilitates the identification of individual chromosome pairs.
back:
• Trypsin digestion followed by Giemsa staining.
• Dark bands: AT-rich, gene-poor, heterochromatic regions.
• Light bands: GC-rich, gene-dense, euchromatic (transcriptionally active) regions.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Contrast the function and count of autosomes versus sex chromosomes in a normal human karyotype.
back:
• Autosomes: 22 pairs (44 total); carry genes for general somatic traits.
• Sex Chromosomes: 1 pair (XX or XY); determine biological sex and secondary sexual characteristics.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the primary structural role of the centromere during mitotic cell division.
back:
• Joins two sister chromatids together.
• Acts as the site for kinetochore assembly.
• Serves as the attachment point for spindle microtubules.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: The normal human diploid genome consists of [___] chromosomes, organized into 23 pairs.
back:
46 chromosomes (23 pairs).
- Includes 22 pairs of autosomes.
- Includes 1 pair of sex chromosomes (XX or XY).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A karyotype performed on a 35-year-old female for prenatal screening shows a normal complement of chromosomes. Identify the sex chromosome pair in this individual.
back:
XX.
- Females possess two X chromosomes.
- Males possess one X and one Y chromosome (XY).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain the role of the centromere in the structure of a metaphase chromosome during karyotyping.
back:
The centromere is the constricted region joining two sister chromatids.
- It serves as the attachment site for spindle fibers.
- Its position defines the chromosome's specific morphology for identification.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: During a laboratory review, a student must distinguish the physical configuration of the 2-meter long genomic DNA from the extrachromosomal DNA found in mitochondria. Contrast these structures.
back:
Nuclear DNA:
- Linear and organized into chromatin/nucleosomes.
Mitochondrial DNA:
- Small, closed, and circular molecules.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Calculate the number of individual autosomes found in a single normal human skin cell.
back:
44 autosomes.
- These represent the 22 pairs of non-sex chromosomes.
- Somatic cells are diploid (2n), containing two full sets.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: The process of systematically ordering and pairing all chromosomes from a cell to provide a genome-wide snapshot of number and structure is known as [___].
back:
Karyotyping.
- Uses staining of metaphase chromosomes.
- Detects numerical (aneuploidy) and large structural (translocation) abnormalities.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: A patient's cytogenetic report indicates '47, XY, +21'. Explain the numerical and structural interpretation of this karyotype.
back:
Total of 47 chromosomes (aneuploidy).
- Male sex (XY).
- Extra copy of chromosome 21 (Trisomy 21).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Explain how cytogeneticists systematically interpret the human karyotype based on chromosome structure and size.
back:
Chromosomes are ordered by decreasing size and centromere location.
- Pairs are identified by specific banding patterns.
- Used to detect deletions, insertions, or translocations.

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Distinguish between diploid (2n) and haploid (n) chromosome numbers in human cells.
back:
Diploid (2n):
- 46 chromosomes; found in somatic cells.
Haploid (n):
- 23 chromosomes; found in germ cells (gametes).

category: Interpret the normal human karyotype in terms of number and structure of chromosomes
front: Identify the specific proteins that provide the positive charge necessary to bind negatively charged DNA into the fundamental structural units of a chromosome.
back:
Histones (H1, H2A, H2B, H3, and H4).
- Rich in basic amino acids (lysine and arginine).
- Form nucleosome cores around which DNA wraps.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A condition where an individual has an exact multiple of the haploid number of chromosomes (e.g., 3n or 4n) is termed [___], whereas an abnormal number that is not an exact multiple (e.g., 2n+1) is called [___].
back: • Polyploidy: The presence of complete extra sets of chromosomes, making the total a multiple of n (e.g., 3n). • Aneuploidy: Gain or loss of individual chromosomes (e.g., 2n+1), typically caused by meiotic nondisjunction.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn presents with a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, and a single palmar crease. Karyotype reveals 47,XX,+21. Explain the most common cytogenetic mechanism responsible for this finding.
back: • Meiotic Nondisjunction: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate. • Usually occurs during maternal oogenesis. • Results in an extra copy of chromosome 21 in all cells of the body.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Describe the structural mechanism of a Robertsonian translocation and identify the specific group of chromosomes involved in this process.
back: • Involves acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, and 22). • Long arms fuse at the centromere; short arms are typically lost. • Balanced carriers have 45 chromosomes but a normal clinical phenotype.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast paracentric and pericentric inversions regarding the involvement of the centromere and their impact on chromosome arm length ratio.
back: • Paracentric: Does not include the centromere; arm ratio remains unchanged. • Pericentric: Includes the centromere; significantly alters the p-to-q arm ratio. • Pericentric inversions often result in unbalanced gametes during meiotic crossover events.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the chromosomal constitution and clinical hallmark features of a male patient presenting with infertility, gynecomastia, and eunuchoid body habitus.
back: • Karyotype: 47,XXY. • Features: Small, firm testes, infertility, and increased stature with long limbs. • Hormonal Profile: Elevated gonadotropins (FSH and LH) due to primary testicular failure and damaged Leydig cells.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The chromosomal abnormality characterized by a 45,X karyotype in a female, resulting in short stature, webbed neck, and streak ovaries, is [___].
back: • Turner Syndrome. • This is the primary cause of female hypogonadism and streak ovaries. • Frequently associated with physical findings like webbed neck, short stature, and cardiovascular defects such as coarctation of the aorta.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn presents with microcephaly, intellectual disability, and a distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry. This phenotype is caused by which specific structural chromosomal abnormality?
back: • Terminal Deletion: Loss of the distal portion of the short arm (p) of chromosome 5. • Notation: 46,XX,del(5p) or 46,XY,del(5p). • Severity of the condition varies depending on the size of the deleted segment.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the mechanism of isochromosome formation during cell division and its effect on gene dosage.
back: • Mechanism: Abnormal transverse cleavage of the centromere instead of longitudinal. • Result: Chromosome with two identical arms (e.g., two q arms). • Outcome: Leads to monosomy for the lost arm and trisomy for the duplicated arm.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Distinguish between reciprocal translocations and Robertsonian translocations based on the exchange of genetic material and resulting chromosome count.
back: • Reciprocal: Segmental exchange between non-homologous chromosomes; count remains 46. • Robertsonian: Fusion of two acrocentric long arms; count reduces to 45. • Robertsonian only involves chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, and 22.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the term used for the presence of two or more cell populations with different genotypes in one individual and identify its developmental cause.
back: • Mosaicism. • Cause: Mitotic nondisjunction during early post-zygotic development. • Clinical Significance: Usually results in a milder clinical phenotype compared to full trisomies due to the presence of normal cell populations in the body.

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The condition characterized by an abnormal number of chromosomes that is not an exact multiple of the haploid set is termed [___].
back:
• Aneuploidy
• Commonly results from non-disjunction during meiosis
• Examples include trisomies (e.g., Down syndrome) or monosomies (e.g., Turner syndrome)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn presents with a flat facial profile, up-slanting palpebral fissures, and a single palmar crease. Cytogenetic analysis is most likely to reveal [___].
back:
• Trisomy 21 (Down Syndrome)
• Most common numerical autosomal abnormality
• Usually caused by meiotic non-disjunction of chromosome 21

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the cellular mechanism of 'non-disjunction' and its typical outcome in gametogenesis.
back:
• Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate
• Occurs during Meiosis I or II
• Results in gametes with extra (n+1) or missing (n-1) chromosomes

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Distinguish between a balanced translocation and an unbalanced translocation regarding their phenotypic impact.
back:
• Balanced: No net loss or gain of genetic material; usually phenotypically normal
• Unbalanced: Loss or gain of segments; results in severe clinical malformations or miscarriage

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the specific type of translocation that occurs only between acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21, 22).
back:
• Robertsonian Translocation
• Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes
• Leads to the loss of short arms (p-arms) containing redundant rRNA genes

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The presence of two or more cell lines with different genotypes in a single individual, arising from post-zygotic mitotic error, is known as [___].
back:
• Mosaicism
• Occurs after fertilization during early cleavage
• Can lead to milder clinical presentations of chromosomal syndromes (e.g., Mosaic Down Syndrome)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A 16-year-old female presents with short stature, primary amenorrhea, and a webbed neck. What is the characteristic numerical abnormality associated with this phenotype?
back:
• 45,X (Turner Syndrome)
• Complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome
• Result of meiotic non-disjunction (often paternal)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the difference between 'paracentric' and 'pericentric' inversions based on the involvement of the centromere.
back:
• Paracentric: Inversion does NOT involve the centromere; both breaks are in one arm
• Pericentric: Inversion involves the centromere; breaks occur in both p and q arms

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast 'polyploidy' with 'aneuploidy' in terms of the total chromosome count.
back:
• Polyploidy: Addition of complete haploid sets (e.g., Triploidy 3n = 69)
• Aneuploidy: Addition or loss of single chromosomes (e.g., 2n + 1 or 2n - 1)

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Identify the standard laboratory technique used to visualize the number and structure of chromosomes in metaphase.
back:
• Karyotyping
• Uses Giemsa staining (G-banding)
• Identifies numerical errors and large structural rearrangements

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A condition where an individual has an extra or missing chromosome, such as Trisomy 21, is technically termed [___].
back: • Aneuploidy • State where a cell has an abnormal number of chromosomes • Primarily arises from meiotic non-disjunction events • Includes common conditions such as trisomy or monosomy

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: A newborn presents with features suggestive of Down syndrome. Karyotyping reveals 46 chromosomes, but one chromosome 14 has an extra piece of chromosome 21 attached. Identify this structural abnormality.
back: • Robertsonian Translocation • Fusion of the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes • The short arms are typically lost without clinical significance • Results in a total count of 45 or 46 chromosomes

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Describe the mechanism of a pericentric inversion and its effect on chromosome structure.
back: • Pericentric Inversion • Occurs when a chromosomal segment breaks at two points and rotates 180 degrees • Includes the centromere within the inverted segment • May alter the p-arm and q-arm length ratio

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Distinguish between chromosomal terminal deletions and interstitial deletions regarding the number of breaks required.
back: • Terminal Deletion involves a single break with loss of the chromosomal tip • Interstitial Deletion requires two breaks within a chromosome arm • Interstitial deletions result in the loss of the internal segment

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Explain the formation of a ring chromosome during chromosomal breakage.
back: • Ring Chromosome • Forms when both telomeric ends of a chromosome break off • The remaining 'sticky' ends of the central portion fuse together • Results in the loss of vital genetic material at the tips

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: The loss of a single chromosome from a diploid set, resulting in a 45,X karyotype in Turner syndrome, is called [___].
back: • Monosomy • The loss of a single chromosome from a pair (2n-1) • Results from non-disjunction in meiosis • Turner syndrome (45,X) is the only viable human example

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Analysis of a patient's cells reveals two distinct cell lines: some with 46,XX and others with 47,XX,+21. Name this phenomenon.
back: • Mosaicism • Occurrence of two or more genetically different cell lines in one individual • Caused by mitotic non-disjunction during early embryonic development • Leads to varying phenotypic severity depending on cell distribution

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Detail the mechanical origin of an isochromosome during cell division.
back: • Isochromosome • Formed by abnormal transverse cleavage of the centromere during division • Results in a chromosome having two identical arms (p or q) • Leads to simultaneous monosomy for one arm and trisomy for the other

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Contrast balanced translocations with unbalanced translocations in terms of net genetic content.
back: • Balanced translocations involve an exchange of segments with no net change in DNA • Unbalanced translocations involve gain or loss of chromosomal segments • Unbalanced forms typically produce severe congenital malformations or lethality

category: Discuss different structural and numerical chromosomal abnormalities
front: Define the term polyploidy as it applies to human numerical chromosomal abnormalities.
back: • Polyploidy • Condition of possessing more than two complete sets of chromosomes • Examples include triploidy (3n=69) or tetraploidy (4n=92) • In humans, this numerical abnormality is almost always lethal
